title: Garak Mall
google_addr: 932 Yangjae-daero, Songpa District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: Lots of meat and seafood produce here at wholesale price. You can buy your produce and have it cooked at the restaurant upstairs. You can even have sashimi at its freshest. The mall was quiet when we arrived at noon.

Seoul evidently has some famous beef/meat markets - and this is one of them.   My family and I came here as part of a tour we booked on AirBNB to purchase our own meat and go to a local place to cook it up (which was a great experience).

I'm not sure I'd recommend coming here on your own as a tourist as there are over 100 small butcher and fish stalls with a huge variety of options.   Our guide walked us through the history of Korean BBQ (started in the 50's), the types of cuts and quality of the beef (lots), and what's considered the best.

He then took us to a certified butcher that caries the best graded beef from female cows and helped us select our cuts.   There's a restaurant at the top of the mall that allows you to cook your own cuts (as long as they're from the market below) and we had a great time eating them all.   My wife and our new friend felt like they came away a bit hungry still so don't be shy about ordering a lot of beef if you go this route.  Our guide recommended 250-350g for average and 400+ for heavy appetites.

All-in-all it was a great experience and delicious meal.  But I wouldn't make this a destination stop.

Bicena has become a place I look forward to returning to, where refined modern Korean cuisine, thoughtful touches, and an elegant atmosphere come together seamlessly.

Elevated Korean Flavors with a Panoramic Vista: A Review of Bicena (Seoul)
Perched on the 81st floor of the iconic Lotte World Tower, Bicena offers a truly breathtaking dining experience, elevating Korean cuisine to new heights both literally and figuratively. From the moment you step into the sophisticated space, you are enveloped in an atmosphere of modern elegance. The dramatic double-height ceilings and expansive panoramic windows immediately draw your eye to the sweeping views of the Seoul skyline, creating an unparalleled backdrop that is as much a part of the experience as the food itself. The interior design thoughtfully blends contemporary aesthetics with subtle Korean sensibilities, fostering a luxurious yet comfortable environment perfect for a memorable occasion.

Bicena's culinary philosophy is centered on presenting contemporary Korean cuisine with an unwavering commitment to authenticity and the integrity of ingredients. Under the guidance of Chef Kwangsik Jun, the kitchen masterfully reinterprets traditional Korean flavors and dishes, infusing them with a refined touch and modern techniques. The restaurant's name, meaning "empty, fill, and share," hints at a philosophy of balance and thoughtful consumption, reflecting a deep respect for both nature's bounty and the communal spirit of Korean dining. This commitment extends to their affiliation with Kwangjuyo, a renowned Korean ceramics company that also produces traditional liquors, emphasizing a holistic appreciation for Korean craftsmanship.

The tasting menu is a curated journey through seasonal delights, showcasing a profound understanding of flavor profiles and textures. Each dish is a testament to meticulous preparation and artistic presentation. You might begin with a delicate welcome drink infused with the refreshing essence of pine needles, setting a serene tone. Highlights often include expertly aged meats, such as pork loin dry-aged with fermented rice salt, cooked to tender perfection and paired with vibrant homemade pickles. Another exquisite example could be crispy barley shrimp, offering a delightful play of textures and a harmonious blend of sweet and savory notes. The use of premium, often locally sourced, ingredients is paramount, ensuring that every bite sings with natural purity. Even traditional elements like rice, soup, and banchan (side dishes) are elevated, appearing as refined components of a cohesive culinary narrative.

The dining experience at Bicena is further enhanced by its impeccable service. The staff are highly attentive, knowledgeable, and move with a quiet efficiency that complements the serene atmosphere. They are adept at guiding guests through the multi-course menu, providing clear and insightful explanations of each dish's inspirations and preparation. This polished hospitality ensures a seamless and enjoyable journey from start to finish. Securing a window table, if possible, adds another layer of magic to the experience, allowing you to dine with Seoul's sprawling panorama as your companion.

In essence, Bicena offers an extraordinary opportunity to experience refined Korean gastronomy. It's a destination where breathtaking views meet exquisite flavors, and where traditional culinary wisdom is gracefully reimagined for the contemporary palate, leaving a lasting impression of sophisticated taste and unforgettable moments.

Hey, let me share something with you for a moment.

Gangdong Arts Center opened back in 2011 and their biggest hall, Hangang, seats about 850 people. It is not a huge place, but maybe that is what gives it its charm. For me, it is close to home, which means I can walk there without stress. Sometimes that little convenience makes all the difference.

I have seen a few performances there. Puccini’s Tosca in October 2023 and Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro in November 2025. Both nights stayed with me, but one of them for an unexpected reason. Right before the opera began, the fire alarm suddenly went off. People were confused, some were frightened, and the staff did not give clear instructions. They later said it was a malfunction, but the moment itself felt unsettling. It is hard to focus on beautiful music right after something like that.

In terms of accessibility, it is much easier than the Seoul Arts Center. Godeok Station on subway line 5 is about a fifteen minute walk away. The box office is on the first floor, and there is a cloak room run by staff. Personally, I like the box seats. They let me concentrate, help me settle into the performance. The seat itself was comfortable, though the earlier chaos stayed with me longer than I expected.

Inside the center, there is a small coffee shop with reasonable prices. Coffee, bread, simple things that make your wait easier. What you will not find is a restaurant, so it is better to eat before you arrive.

Small hall, easy access, a few rough edges, but still a place where art lives.

title: Gangbyeon Spa Land
google_addr: 45 Guuigangbyeon-ro, Gwangjin District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: Came here for the first time 5 years ago and happy to report it's stil going strong. There are many different hot rooms in the jjimjilbang area and the relaxing zone is very spacious. Plus these little nooks that I haven't seen anywhere else.

A bit outside of the city centre - it's a bus ride and then a 5-10 minutes walk - but it is one of the best jjimjilbang (relaxation centres) and Korean spas in Seoul in terms of the different facilities, and it is open 24/7.

Be aware that the majority of people who go there are local Koreans, not tourists, so very little (if any) English is spoken. However, the staff were super helpful and welcoming to me when I went (mid-week in the middle of the day, when it wasn't too busy compared to evenings and weekends).

At street level, look for the green and white sign with the red spa logo, then head down 2 flights of steps. Pay at the machine at the entrance: either the day price (spa only or spa + jjimjilbang) or night price; male or female; adult or child. Take the ticket, which indicates your locker number.

You have to be barefoot in the spa, so take your shoes off at the entrance, and place these in the relevant numbered (male/female) shoe locker. Place the key band on your wrist. This is also the key for your changing room locker and the dongle to scan for any extras (food; massages; facials; massage chairs, etc), which you pay for at the end of your stay.

Take the ticket to the reception desk. If you have paid for the jjimjilbang as well as the spa, then you will be given some lounging pyjamas in addition to towels. The spas are segregated (male/female); the jjimjilbang areas are not.

Go first to the male or female changing room for the spa. Strip naked and place all your belongings in your locker (NOTE: these are big enough to fit a slim cabin-sized trolley bag, but not larger suitcases or backpacks).

Go first to the stand-up showers in the spa area, and thoroughly wash and scrub yourself from top to toe. Riverside does not provide any toiletries, but does have items for sale at a stall in the changing rooms if you have not brought your own. Once you are thoroughly clean, you can use the spa facilities, which include various different bathing pools at different temperatures and wet saunas. Before leaving the spa area, shower and scrub yourself thoroughly again, but at the sit-down showers.

Once you have dried off, put on the lounging pyjamas, and head upstairs to the jjimjilbang area. In addition to the main common area and sleeping spaces, the lounging areas include various different dry sauna spaces (yellow clay kiln; salt rock kiln; silver room; hot kiln; charcoal room; pine wood room, etc); igloo room; more massage treatment rooms; study area; play area for kids; games room; exercise room; massage chairs and foot massage machines.

There is a cafe that serves typical jjimjilbang snacks and refreshments (ramyeon noodles; hard boiled eggs; icecreams; a sweet rice drink called sikhye...), and a second cafe that does typical Korean meals.

title: Galleria Department Store Luxury Hall
google_name: Galleria Department Store Luxury Hall WEST
google_addr: 343 Apgujeong-ro, Gangnam District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: There is a fine supermarket with many food stalls downstairs. I've tried strawberries around Seoul, but the ones they sold were the best!

This department store truly stands out for offering some of the best services compared to others.

First, their valet service sets the tone. Unlike many places where you need to be a VIP customer to enjoy that convenience, here it’s available to everyone. It makes the whole experience of visiting the store feel effortless from the very start.

Second, the food court is on another level. Instead of the usual chains or generic options, the restaurants are often popular, trendy spots that, in their original locations, are known for long wait times. Dining here gives you the same experience without the hassle of waiting in line. I also appreciate their system: you order, place your pager on the table, and the staff deliver the food directly to you. When you’re finished, they clear everything away. One of the biggest reasons I disliked eating at department stores before was the contradiction of paying high prices only to serve myself and return the tray—like at a fast-food place. Thankfully, Galleria does things differently, making the whole experience feel worthy of the price.

Third, the staff expertise is remarkable. They actually know what they’re selling. I once had a frustrating experience at another department store where a staff member recommended what I thought was French cheese, but it turned out to be butter. She didn’t understand the product herself, and worse, recommended something completely wrong. That kind of mistake would never happen here—the staff at Galleria are knowledgeable and professional, and it makes a big difference in the shopping experience.

Lastly, their grocery section feels curated rather than overwhelming. Instead of a massive selection, the products are carefully edited, almost as if they only stock what they consider the best produce, fruits, and specialty goods. The downside is that the prices are steep—sometimes even ridiculously so. But still, there are a few items I can only find here, which keeps me coming back despite the premium.

The palace was built in the 15th century during the Joseon Dynasty., but then burned down during the Japanese invasion in the 16th century, and reconstructed soon afterwards to serve as the main residence of the kings for the next 250 years. The layout of the palace and the surroundings follows the Confucian principles with gates, courts, and residential areas, as exemplified by the similar but much larger Forbidden City in Beijing. The palace had an important influence on Korean architecture and garden design, as can be seen when visiting Seoul's many other places.

Beautiful place to walk around and experience traditional Seoul. The hanok houses, narrow alleys, and city views make it feel like stepping back in time, especially early in the morning when it’s quiet.

Bukchon Hanok Village is easy to combine with Gyeongbokgung Palace in a day trip. The bus drops you right at Bukchon-ro, where maps help you plan your walk. The village sits on a hillside, so expect some gentle climbs, but the backstreets reveal clusters of traditional hanok homes, rooftop views, and even glimpses of Gyeongbokgung Palace. There are cozy cafes with terraces for a break. Best to allow at least 2 hours to explore and find photo spots. Keep in mind it’s a residential area with access limited to 10 am–5 pm, so be respectful when taking photos. Still, it’s worth a visit for the atmosphere and views.

Hey there, let me share a little baseball story with you.

Gocheok Sky Dome is the home of the Kiwoom Heroes. Sounds exciting, right? The catch is that getting there is not so simple. It sits far from the center of Seoul, and if you are like me, not familiar with this corner of the city, it feels like a bit of a journey.

The real challenge comes with Line 1 of the subway. That line is always crowded, always confusing. I have been to this stadium five times, and still I get lost. One wrong move on the train and you could find yourself in Incheon or Seodongtan. I know, because it happened to me.

As for the Dome itself, it is not huge. Sixteen thousand seats in total, which is less than half the size of Kyocera Dome in Osaka that holds more than thirty-six thousand. Still, what it lacks in scale, it makes up for in condition. The place is clean, modern, and well kept.

Before you go inside, take a moment at the entrance. You will see the large Sky Dome sign, and right nearby, a small official shop where you can pick up Kiwoom Heroes merchandise. A nice stop for souvenirs. Security will check your bag and scan your ticket, nothing out of the ordinary.

Inside, the food is straightforward. Think fast food and drinks, the kind that keep you going through nine innings. It is not fine dining, but it does the job.

So, is it worth the trip? Maybe yes, maybe no. But if you love baseball, or if you simply want to add another stadium to your list, then yes, it is worth the effort. Just double-check that you are on the right train.

reviews.text:
The Bronze Age tomb in Gocheok-dong, Guro-gu, Seoul.
Gocheok-dong dolmens are located in the mountain behind Gocheok High School at San 12-1, Gocheok-dong, Guro-gu, Seoul, and in the Saturn compound of Sinjeong-ri, the Saturn of the Three Kingdoms period.
The Gocheok-dong dolmens were first discovered by the Seoul National University investigation team in 1998, but no formal academic investigation has been conducted. Subsequently, in the investigation of related scholars, it was suggested that "the stones of the same shape as the cover stone do not exist around the cover stone, so they appear to have deviated from their original position." In addition, although the scale is not large, the stone room has been confirmed, and it is presumed to be a dolmens based on the arrangement of stones.
It is estimated to be a foundation stone tomb, and the size of the cover stone is 190cm wide, 105cm long, and 28cm high, and the lump stone is 50cm long and 12cm wide, which is not large.
There are no artifacts excavated directly around the dolmen.
Currently, the management is in good condition, such as installing information boards and protective fences to protect the Jiseok tomb.
Gocheok-dong dolmens are the only dolmens in Guro-gu, and they are good materials for understanding the cultural aspects of the surrounding areas of the Bronze Age, along with the nearby Gocheok-dong relic distribution sites.

Statues in Children's Grand Park
Song Jin-woo (宋鎭禹, May 8, 1890 – December 30, 1945) was a Korean independence activist and politician who worked as a journalist, educator, thinker, and politician during the Japanese occupation and shortly after liberation
He was the first leader of the Democratic Party of Korea (黨 of the People's Republic of Korea) and was one of the 48 national representatives during the March 1 Independence Movement in 1919.
After studying in Japan, he returned to Korea and took over the Central School with Kim Seong-soo, and took over as vice-principalbecame the principal in February 1919. Inspired by Woodrow Wilson's national self-determinationism, he was arrested as one of the 48 national representatives who led the March 1st Movement in 1919, and was acquitted by a second trial, released after a year and a half of unsentenced detention, and later transformed into a realist. In 1920, he was caught by the police who were monitoring him while he was raising funds for the establishment of the school. After that, he founded the Dong-A Ilbo with Kim Sung-soo and others, served as president, chief editor, and advisor of the Dong-A Ilbo, and supported the Bnarod movement by participating in the product promotion movement and the civil university foundation movement under the belief that fostering skills would bring about national independence. After the Pacific War, he refused to cooperate with Chang's family name under the pretext of illness, and was liberated in August 1945

The staff were professional yet warm, and everything from boarding to the safety instructions and cruise duration was well organized. I appreciated how clean and well-maintained the yacht was—modern, spacious, and picture-perfect. Whether you're planning a romantic date, a small celebration, or want to see Seoul from a different perspective, this place is a fantastic choice.

Golden Blue Marina is more than a yacht club; it’s a peaceful retreat, a photography paradise, and a place to create beautiful memories.

title: 80th Anniversary of Korea's Liberation 'Walking the Path of Victims of Compulsory Mobilization'
google_name: National Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation
google_addr: Daeyeon-dong, Nam-gu, Busan, South Korea

reviews.text:
It's basically the holocaust museum for the Japanese occupation of Korea. For those who don't know, Japan took over large parts of Asia and forced (or enslaved) millions of people to work for the purpose of building its empire. This museum seeks to document the history and individual stories of survivors of the Japanese rule. If you loved Schindler's List, then you might find yourself interested in what happened here.

It's free and well worth it if you have the time and are interested. However, it's kind of hard to bring young children here even though they have a room for children on the 7th floor.

A very good museum on an important subject that shows how the ghosts of history haunt the present. Admission is free.

I expected more of the permanent exhibition would be dedicated to telling the history of the so-called ‘comfort women’, not least their struggle to reintegrate into society after the war. I thought that this particular aspect of forced mobilization wasn’t explored deeply enough.

The permanent exhibition museum can be repetitive in sections, and there are some seemingly serious factual discrepancies: see my photos of two nearby panels that variously claim 209,000 and 400,000 Koreans were mobilized as soldiers until liberation. In general, the English language descriptions would benefit from an English proofreader.

But overall, it’s a must-see when you’re in South Korea if you want to understand the country’s history and relationship with Japan. I also commend the museum for recognizing the many efforts of Japanese citizens and historians to uncover the truth and hold their conservative governments to account.
Very sad, it's a must vist. It helped my understanding of the Koreans suffering, at the hands of the Japanese.
Really interesting museum, I didn’t know much about the forced work, the “comfort women” and the atrocities that Japanese did in Korea in the years prior and during the II World War

Visited the National Theater of Korea and was thoroughly impressed! The place is huge, offering multiple performance halls that host a variety of traditional and contemporary shows. The facilities, including bathrooms, are well-maintained, and the lawns are spotlessly cared for, creating a welcoming environment. We enjoyed some beverages from the nearby cafe, which were delightful. Additionally, the accessibility is top-notch with a bus stop right in front that makes it super convenient for visitors. I’ve been to the National Theater of Korea a few times now. I watched La Traviata last September, Joyous Resonance in January, and L’italiana in Algeri in February. Each show was different, but they all had that moment when the lights dim, the orchestra begins, and the whole room breathes together. That’s the part I love most.

The theater is one of the biggest in Korea. It went through a renovation in 2021, and it looks great. The halls are clean, the seats are comfortable, and everything feels new. Still, I think a great theater needs more than just a nice building. It needs warmth. It needs to feel like a place made for people, not just for performances.

If you are planning to visit with kids, there is something you should know. Getting there is not easy. The theater sits halfway up Namsan Mountain, right in the middle of Seoul but far from the subway. The nearest station, Dongguk University on Line 3, is not within walking distance. You have to take a bus, usually number 420. Now, imagine yourself holding your child and a bag while standing on a crowded bus on your way to an opera. You will probably be tired before you even get there.

That is why I think accessibility matters. A public theater should welcome people from the moment they decide to come, not make them wonder how to reach it.

Once you are inside, things get better. The space feels open and organized. There are four floors, labeled L, 1, 2, and 3. Each one has vending machines for water and soft drinks. On the L floor, there is a restaurant called Central Yunit. It looks comfortable and has many seats, although it seems a bit expensive. There is also a KB Bank ATM nearby, which is convenient.

The box office is on the 1st floor, which feels like the 2nd floor if you are used to the American floor system. There is a small café that sells sandwiches and coffee, and the box office opens one hour before the show. The staff are calm and polite. You can leave your coat in the cloakroom across from the counter. They put a numbered sticker on the back of your ticket so you can pick it up easily after the show.

There are plenty of seats for intermission, and the atmosphere stays quiet and comfortable. After the performance, shuttle buses take people back to Dongguk University Station and Dongdaemun History and Culture Park Station. If you miss one, another comes in about twenty minutes.

Yes, getting there takes effort, but once you sit down and the music starts, you forget about all of that. The voices rise, the stage glows, and for a while, everything else fades away. That is the beauty of live performance, and it is why I keep coming back.

The museum itself is clean, beautifully laid out, and very foreigner friendly. The overall energy feels calm, intentional, and elevated. And the museum shop is honestly one of the best I have ever experienced anywhere in the world. The curation, design objects, and gifts are exceptional.

reviews.text:
A little over a month ago, I finally crossed the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Seoul off my must-visit list. As a venue dedicated to showcasing both established masters and the vibrant contemporary scene, the MMCA is a truly world-class institution.
The most satisfying aspect of the visit was finally standing before works that feel legendary. Nam June Paik's Junk TV (잡동사니 벽) is an anarchic, mesmerizing wall of visual noise that beautifully captures the artist's genius and prescience regarding media overload. It remains a chaotic, vital masterpiece that anchors the modern collection.
Equally compelling, though in a profoundly quieter way, was Do Ho Suh's Floor. The simple act of walking across the glass surface, supported by hundreds of tiny, straining figures, transforms the space into an interactive, existential metaphor. It's a testament to Suh's ability to imbue architectural space with deep, personal meaning.
However, the highlight of the visit, and a thrilling discovery for me, was Jung Yeondoo's Cinemagician. Experiencing this piece for the first time was genuinely captivating. Jung has a powerful way of blending the real and the imagined, and Cinemagician offered a fresh perspective on narrative and memory. It was the perfect example of the MMCA's strength: honoring foundational artists while actively championing the next generation of visionary creators.
The collection is diverse, the curation is thoughtful, and the combination of monumental installations and unexpected delights makes it an absolutely essential stop for anyone interested in contemporary art.

We visited last year and were a bit disappointed in the exhibits. Our friend convinced us to attend this year as Kim Tschang-yeul was showing and we are so glad we did. The National Assembly building is where members of the National Assembly discuss state affairs. It includes various buildings of the National Assembly, including the main conference hall, committee conference rooms, the Speaker's residence, the Members' Hall, the security building, and the vehicle maintenance depot. It was completed in August 1975 after 6 years of construction, and is a modern building style with traditional Korean beauty. The 24 pillars surrounding the National Assembly building represent the diverse opinions of the people, and the dome roof symbolizes the essence of parliamentary democracy, where the people's opinions are discussed for and against and then come to a conclusion.

reviews.text: My trip started on a high at Sejong Theatre, where I watched the musical Phantom. The performance was absolutely stunning—the set, the music, the voices. For a couple of hours, I was so absorbed I didn’t even check my phone (which, let’s be honest, says a lot for a Gen Z like me). It felt like stepping into a different world, and I left with goosebumps.

My time exploring Sejong Plaza was spent enjoying the beautiful statue of Sejong the Great. There's many animations on the buildings, hidden alley restaurants that are ALL 10/10, and subway/public transportation hub.

The Sejong Center for the Performing Arts is an iconic performance venue located in Gwanghwamun, Seoul. For Korean artists, performing here is considered the ultimate honor, and it wouldn't be an exaggeration to call it the Carnegie Hall of Korea. While the facilities are somewhat dated and inconvenient, they are receiving positive feedback. It is conveniently located right next to Gwanghwamun Square, and it is also great for a walk after the performance. Making its own original performances like Ilmu(One Dance) is also a promising idea.

Exhibition
Masterpieces from the San Diego Museum of Art: "From the Renaissance to Impressionism"

Hey, let me share a quick thought with you.

If you ever find yourself near Gwanghwamun, take a moment to walk by the Sejong Center. And if you already have a ticket in hand, even better. You are about to step into one of Korea’s most meaningful performance halls.

Sejong Center has long been considered a symbol of Korean performing arts. When it opened in 1978, its pipe organ was the largest in Asia. Back in Europe, pipe organs were a way for cities to show their pride and prosperity, and Sejong Center carried that same spirit here in Seoul.

Sure, some people might say it is not the most modern venue anymore. And they would not be completely wrong. But this place holds memories. It has watched generations grow up, quietly standing its ground while the city changed around it. That kind of history matters.

Personally, I have spent some memorable nights here. I watched THE GREATEST: Thrill with Jeong Dong-ha and Sohyang in September 2023, Universal Ballet’s The Nutcracker in December 2023, and Chung Myung-Whun conducting Beethoven’s Ninth with the KBS Symphony at the end of 2025. Since it is a multipurpose hall, you might not always get the same powerful acoustics as a dedicated concert hall, especially for classical music. Still, the experience feels special every time.

Getting there is easy. Just hop on Seoul Subway Line 5 and get off at Gwanghwamun Station. One small thing to note, though. There is no traditional cloakroom. Instead, you will find unmanned lockers on the second floor. They work, but the touch screen can be a little tricky. Maybe it is just me getting older.

The box office is on the first floor, and there are kiosks if you already bought your ticket. You will also spot vending machines for water on each floor, which always comes in handy.

One last tip. The Grand Theater usually opens about two hours before the performance for security reasons, and audiences are allowed into the hall about thirty minutes before the show starts.

Take your time, soak it in, and enjoy the moment.

I found Girin while researching arm liposuction in Seoul and comparing multiple clinics. I read a lot of reviews and carefully checked before-and-after photos. During my consultation, everything was explained clearly including realistic expectations, swelling, downtime, and recovery discomfort. I appreciated that Dr. Lee Jong Ho was straightforward and did not overpromise results. My upper arms have always been an area that didn’t slim down proportionally, even when I lost weight. I wanted a more refined and balanced silhouette, especially in sleeveless clothing. After thinking about it for a long time, I decided liposuction was the right solution rather than continuing to try to spot-reduce through diet or exercise.

After the consultation with Dr. Lee Jong Ho, I felt confident moving forward. I didn’t feel pressured, just informed. On surgery day, the team was organized and reassuring. I was nervous, but the staff made the process feel structured and professional from start to finish.

For the Healing Process, the first 1–2 days were the most uncomfortable. I experienced significant soreness (similar to intense muscle soreness), swelling, tightness, and limited arm mobility. It was difficult to lift my arms high enough to wash my face or brush my hair at first.

Worth a visit if you are visiting the area and wish to observe a local market.

title: Namsan Octagonal Pavilion

reviews.text: Namsan Palgakjeong is a peaceful retreat with stunning views of Seoul’s skyline. The octagonal pavilion’s intricate design adds a touch of tradition amidst the city buzz. While it can get busy, it’s a great spot to catch your breath after a hike or cable car ride. Stay for sunset if you can—the blend of colors over the city is truly unforgettable and worth the visit.

Its another 🆓 spot in same vicinity as namsan tower.

We came here during late afternoon early evening on a pretty sunny day. It was a nice spot to sit down and cool off and take in the views and people watch.

Its visually pleasing and wasnt crowded either given that it was pretty busy otherwise at the base of namsan.

Hope to see it during night time views whenever i visit next. (Hopefully soon)

It is so beautiful. I never expected there was a traditional resting zone over here. That was cool. This traditional zone is called the Octagonal Pavilion. The name sounds so cool too. There are many people sitting over there at that time. I guarantee I will come here again in the future.

Originally known as Unamjeong Pavilion, the pavilion was built in 1959 to commemorate Rhee Syngman. It was demolished by the 4.19 movement in 1960 and was rebuilt on November 11, 1968.

A great place to take in the culture and history of Namsan mountain.
Great spot to take pictures of the city without spending the hefty amounts of money to get to the top of the Tower. The view is pretty unobstructed here already.

title: Namsangol Park Seoul Millennium Time Capsule Plaza

reviews.text: This beautiful, quiet park is the perfect place to escape the noisy city. There’s so many different paths and places to sit and relax. It’s also never very busy!

Quiet and beautiful place with plenty of greenery. The traditional Korean atmosphere feels very authentic and calming. The fact that entry is completely free makes it even more impressive. It is perfect for a short visit, and a simple thirty minute walk through the park already feels rewarding. I highly recommend stopping by if you are in the area.

Namsagol Park is a hidden gem for those who want to escape the hustle and bustle of the city. With its serene atmosphere and picturesque scenery, it's the perfect place to take a leisurely stroll. Although it's not a well-known tourist spot, it's a popular destination for locals who want to unwind and relax. On a sunny day, the park comes alive with vibrant colors and the sound of nature. I highly recommend visiting Namsagol Park if you're looking for a peaceful retreat in the middle of the city.
This is a nice place to end your tour after Hanok Village. Lots of instagrammable corners left and right. You can completely relax after walking down the historical Hanok village.
Great place to see cherry blossoms in the spring! A nice park with a fairly unique layout and a hanok village inside.

title: Namsangol Hanok Village
google_addr: 28 Toegye-ro 34-gil, Jung District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text:
A truly peaceful and beautiful place where time feels slower. From here, you can even see the Seoul Tower, which makes the view even more special.

I visited early in the morning, and it was the best decision — there were hardly five people around. The ambiance was extremely calm and quiet. After 9 AM, the crowd slowly starts coming in, so going early is highly recommended to experience the serenity.

Walking inside and around every corner of the village feels refreshing and soothing. Each side has its own charm, with traditional houses, open spaces, and nature coming together so beautifully.

The staff members were very kind and welcoming, adding warmth to the overall experience. This is a perfect place to walk slowly, explore every part of the village, and truly enjoy a peaceful moment in the city.

~throw back to mid of November 2025~

If you love Korean culture and tradition, this is a great place to visit.
The entire area isn’t very large, and I spent about 1.5 hours leisurely walking around, exploring, and taking photos.

We stumbled upon this curious place almost by accident.

In fact, the village is only relatively historical. On the one hand, houses from the Joseon dynasty era were brought here from all over the city. On the other hand, there was no such village here before, it was created artificially.

So, it is a collection of many old buildings gathered in one place, allowing visitors to explore a concentrated snapshot of architecture from a bygone era.

I am no expert in architecture, so I simply enjoyed wandering around the village, looking at the houses, and trying to imagine what life was like in a traditional Korean village.

The place is beautiful and not overly crowded with tourists.

Surrounding the village, just like near many other attractions, are only modern buildings, which somewhat detracts from the historical ambiance -)

It is an interesting place where you can enjoy a leisurely walk and admire the old houses.

This sight is so pretty, never crowded in any of the times I have visited it, with gorgeous views of Namsan tower. I don't get the hullabaloo in the residential Bukchon Hanok Village where tourists get on the nerves of the locals, when this one fullfils the purpose better.

Beautiful scenery for a nice walk, to read a book, or to take amazing photos. Entry was free. Traditional Hanok houses, mini forest trails, water features, monuments, views of Namsan and the Seoul Tower all in one spot.

title: Namsan Park (Seoul)
google_addr: 231 Samil-daero, Jung District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text:
N Seoul Tower is one of the best places to enjoy a full panoramic view of Seoul. From the observation deck, you can see the Han River, modern skyscrapers, and the entire city spread out below, especially beautiful at sunset and at night when the city lights come on.

The area around the tower is clean and well organized, with many photo spots, the famous love locks area, and cafés to relax. The cable car is convenient, but walking up the mountain is also a great option if you enjoy nature and fresh air.

The staff are friendly and the signs are clear, making it easy for visitors to get around. This is a must-visit place in Seoul, perfect for couples, families, and anyone who wants to experience the romantic atmosphere of the city.

We came in winter and it was a cold cloudy dark windy day. It was depressingly brown so this affected my review

This is the lower area of Namsam Tower and it didn't feel like a park

The cable car to the top was not operating due to high winds and it was a bit to slippery to hike up
So we did not get to see the tower part which is supposed to be spectacular.
Very nice park in the 명동 area of Seoul. I enjoyed another hike after eating lunch close by. Very scenic with nice fall breeze on a Monday afternoon. Pretty views everywhere and it wasn’t too crowded.

I was fortunate to make the long walk (around 5km), easy to west, twice in the last week. Up from the east part, starting at Dongguk University Station and Jangchungdan Park up through Seoul Namsan Park to the tower and then down to Myeong-dong on the west site. It's strikingly beautiful a great climb, some steps are numbered, between those and the ones you don't count I imagine it's the equivalent to about 1,000 steps up the mountain and there are also a few steeper inclines. The steps, paths and roads are in excellent condition, everything is so clean and well signposted in many languages. You can also use N aver Maps to get you there.

The walk from Dongguk University Station to the base of Namsan Seoul Tower covers approximately 2.2 miles (3.6 km) with an elevation gain of about 797 feet (243 meters).

This route is one of the most rewarding ways to reach Namsan Tower, especially if you're seeking a blend of urban forest, cultural landmarks, and a bit of cardio. If you're up for it, you can extend your walk along the Namsan Trail network, which spans nearly 8 km across the mountain.

Outstanding urban park perfect for walking, running, and cycling! Features multiple trails and beautiful paved, hilly roads with stunning viewpoints. Well-maintained with convenient public facilities. The place comes alive at 5am with enthusiastic athletes - such great energy! Plenty of shaded areas to rest. A true urban gem!

There was an exhibition venue called Memory 6, but unfortunately, it was closed from September 2024 to the present (March 2025) due to the installation of Namsan Gondora. title: Namsan Seoul Tower
addr: 105 Namsan Park-gil, Yongsan-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea
google_addr: 105 Namsangongwon-gil, Yongsan District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: Lots of people haha. Exit queue line very very long. However I enjoy the experience on the top observation viewing. The sunset view is stunning. The climbing is really a hell . As we didn’t board any bus up . But five star for the facilities:)

Hiking up Namsan can be a bit challenging because the path is quite steep. Even though I’m in my 30s, I still found myself catching my breath while walking up. My friend suggested a funny trick,walking up while facing slightly backward,which actually made the climb feel a little easier.

Despite the steep hike, the experience is worth it. The view from Namsan is beautiful, the air is cool, and the atmosphere feels very romantic. It’s a great place to enjoy the scenery, take photos, and spend time with someone special.

Overall, Namsan is a lovely spot to visit, especially for couples and lovers who want a romantic walk with a wonderful view.

The iconic N Seoul Tower and definitely a must visit when you are in Seoul. It is one of those places you really have to see at least once. The view from the top is amazing and gives you a great look over the city, especially at night when everything is lit up. There are lots of activities around the area, places to walk, take photos, and just enjoy the atmosphere. It is a good spot to spend a few hours and really take in the experience. A very memorable and iconic part of Seoul.

I hiked up to Seoul North Tower and walked all 1,000 stairs to the top. The trail is beautiful with all the fall colors and the air feels so fresh. Someone even marked the stair count along the way, which kept me going. I went up for the 5:15 sunset and I was definitely ambitious because I barely made it on time. The view over Seoul is absolutely breathtaking.

The stairs are very well maintained and there are little resting spots every few minutes. At the top there is a plaza, a 7-Eleven, and a restaurant. After watching the sunset it got dark really fast, and that’s when I realized I couldn’t get an Uber to come up. What an adventure. It was an amazing hike and I highly recommend it. Just make sure your T-money card has enough balance if you stay late! 😅

title: Namsan Circulation Interchange Road

reviews.text:
N Seoul Tower is one of the best places to enjoy a full panoramic view of Seoul. From the observation deck, you can see the Han River, modern skyscrapers, and the entire city spread out below, especially beautiful at sunset and at night when the city lights come on.

The area around the tower is clean and well organized, with many photo spots, the famous love locks area, and cafés to relax. The cable car is convenient, but walking up the mountain is also a great option if you enjoy nature and fresh air.

The staff are friendly and the signs are clear, making it easy for visitors to get around. This is a must-visit place in Seoul, perfect for couples, families, and anyone who wants to experience the romantic atmosphere of the city.

We came in winter and it was a cold cloudy dark windy day. It was depressingly brown so this affected my review

This is the lower area of Namsam Tower and it didn't feel like a park

So we did not get to see the tower part which is supposed to be spectacular.
Very nice park in the 명동 area of Seoul. I enjoyed another hike after eating lunch close by. Very scenic with nice fall breeze on a Monday afternoon. Pretty views everywhere and it wasn’t too crowded.

I was fortunate to make the long walk (around 5km), easy to west, twice in the last week. Up from the east part, starting at Dongguk University Station and Jangchungdan Park up through Seoul Namsan Park to the tower and then down to Myeong-dong on the west site. It's strikingly beautiful a great climb, some steps are numbered, between those and the ones you don't count I imagine it's the equivalent to about 1,000 steps up the mountain and there are also a few steeper inclines. The steps, paths and roads are in excellent condition, everything is so clean and well signposted in many languages. You can also use N aver Maps to get you there.

The walk from Dongguk University Station to the base of Namsan Seoul Tower covers approximately 2.2 miles (3.6 km) with an elevation gain of about 797 feet (243 meters).

This route is one of the most rewarding ways to reach Namsan Tower, especially if you're seeking a blend of urban forest, cultural landmarks, and a bit of cardio. If you're up for it, you can extend your walk along the Namsan Trail network, which spans nearly 8 km across the mountain.

Outstanding urban park perfect for walking, running, and cycling! Features multiple trails and beautiful paved, hilly roads with stunning viewpoints. Well-maintained with convenient public facilities. The place comes alive at 5am with enthusiastic athletes - such great energy! Plenty of shaded areas to rest. A true urban gem!

title: A cultural game centered on Namsan Mountain
google_addr: 28 Toegye-ro 34-gil, Jung District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text:
A truly peaceful and beautiful place where time feels slower. From here, you can even see the Seoul Tower, which makes the view even more special.

I visited early in the morning, and it was the best decision — there were hardly five people around. The ambiance was extremely calm and quiet. After 9 AM, the crowd slowly starts coming in, so going early is highly recommended to experience the serenity.

Walking inside and around every corner of the village feels refreshing and soothing. Each side has its own charm, with traditional houses, open spaces, and nature coming together so beautifully.

The staff members were very kind and welcoming, adding warmth to the overall experience. This is a perfect place to walk slowly, explore every part of the village, and truly enjoy a peaceful moment in the city.

~throw back to mid of November 2025~

If you love Korean culture and tradition, this is a great place to visit.
The entire area isn’t very large, and I spent about 1.5 hours leisurely walking around, exploring, and taking photos.

We stumbled upon this curious place almost by accident.

In fact, the village is only relatively historical. On the one hand, houses from the Joseon dynasty era were brought here from all over the city. On the other hand, there was no such village here before, it was created artificially.

So, it is a collection of many old buildings gathered in one place, allowing visitors to explore a concentrated snapshot of architecture from a bygone era.

I am no expert in architecture, so I simply enjoyed wandering around the village, looking at the houses, and trying to imagine what life was like in a traditional Korean village.

The place is beautiful and not overly crowded with tourists.

Surrounding the village, just like near many other attractions, are only modern buildings, which somewhat detracts from the historical ambiance -)

It is an interesting place where you can enjoy a leisurely walk and admire the old houses.

This sight is so pretty, never crowded in any of the times I have visited it, with gorgeous views of Namsan tower. I don't get the hullabaloo in the residential Bukchon Hanok Village where tourists get on the nerves of the locals, when this one fullfils the purpose better.

Beautiful scenery for a nice walk, to read a book, or to take amazing photos. Entry was free. Traditional Hanok houses, mini forest trails, water features, monuments, views of Namsan and the Seoul Tower all in one spot.

reviews.text:

This was the first time we took a tethered helium balloon. We chose to come in the evening at 5pm. The ground staff were helpful; making sure that we filled up the necessary documents correctly. The "pilots" were cheerful and made sure that we were evenly spread before taking off. The evening sky was  colorful and lovely. The "ride" was smooth. When the balloon slowly escalated, we were treated to breath-taking views. The balloon was so stable that taking photos was not difficult at all. Strongly recommend this fun memorable activity.

This is such a fun way to see Seoul from a completely different perspective than you’d get at Seoul N Tower or Lotte World Tower. We reserved our tickets online in advance (recommended, since space is limited), but you can also buy them on site.

After a short safety video and signing the consent form, you’re lifted 426 feet into the air, and it really does feel high up! The views were spectacular, and it gave me a new appreciation for just how beautiful Seoul is. The ride itself is for 15 minutes but you will want to budget about an hour end to end. Yeouido, where this is located, is also a lovely area to explore.

Afterwards, you can stop by The Hyundai Seoul nearby to stroll around or grab a bite to eat. If you want to experience Seoul from a true bird’s-eye view, I definitely recommend trying this.

title: Crossing me to the forest library

reviews.text:
Crossing Me to the Forest Library is a library in Eunpyeong-gu that opened on June 21, 2018. The library was created to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the birth of Yun Dong-ju, a resistance poet and independence activist in Japanese colonial era. The name 'crossing me to the forest' is a quote from poet Yun Dong-ju's 'New Road'. For your information, Soongsil High School, poet Yun Dong-ju's alma mater, is located near the library building.

As it is a new library, the overall facilities are very fresh and clean. Its unique design is different from the exterior, interior facilities, and general libraries. There are many spaces decorated with cute props, and on the second floor, there was also an exhibition hall where you can find out the life story of poet Yun Dong-ju.

There was no reading room with a partition, but it is a facility that is not lacking even if it is for learning purposes. It's great to stay with a fresh and distant atmosphere thanks to a theme mostly made of white. The children's/infant archives were rather small, but it's good that they're that far away.

The design of the library, which was created to honor and correspond to poet Yun Dong-ju, was also quite unique and unique. If you travel to Eunpyeong-gu, it is a library worth visiting at least once.
It is a quiet and clean library. On the second floor, there is also the Yun Bong-ju Poet Exhibition Hall. The parking lot is rather small, so I recommend you not to take your car with you.

I'll go often!

reviews.text:
I had the best and freshest seafood here at a remarkably reasonable price. A tip: know what you want and order it directly, otherwise the friendly ahjumma and ahjussi might enthusiastically try to offer you everything they have!

The sashimi and crab were absolutely to die for—incredibly fresh, with a natural sweetness that really shone through. An outstanding meal.

I have mixed feelings about this place. On one hand the seafood is top notch but just the idea that you know prices will be hiked up makes one think if we are getting fleeced.

That said it is competitive so I woke recommend walking around to get a feel of the prices before deciding. Once you’ve settled the purchase of the items, they’ll bring you up to the affiliated restaurant so they can cook it.

The meal after is pretty good, as usual! Fresh king crab and good sashimi. Always order the  ramyeon and fried rice. Overall, it was v delish. But you just gotta go through the buying process first!

Noryangjin Fish Market is a place I occasionally visit for sashimi. It's been a while since I last visited, and it's much cleaner than before, with parking much easier. And there's almost no solicitation like there used to be, so I can walk around comfortably, browse, and get my sashimi. It's not close, but there are few places in Seoul where you can get sashimi at such a good price. I'll have to come back often whenever I crave sashimi.

I had a positive experience here as a tourist. Lots of the stalls were trying to get us to buy their stuff which is expected. Hard to walk around without someone trying to get you to buy their stuff. Most stalls seemed to sell the same stuff. The people selling just fish in the back weren’t as pushy and helped us find someone selling eel which was all the way in the back. The stall we went to the lady was nice and picked out a crab for me. I believe it was 100000 won. She also gave me clams for service as well. Then a man took us to the second floor restaurant which steamed the crab and bbq our eel. We even got the crab head fried rice. I don’t remember the price for cooking but I don’t think it was a lot like some people said they charge tourists. Overall a great experience for a seafood lover.

Noryangjin Fish Market is huge! You could easily spend hours walking from stall to stall comparing prices! Instead, we decided to go with one stall we felt comfortable with (and with no language barrier). To our surprise, many of the sellers could speak Chinese quite well, which made communication much easier!

There are so many seafood choices that you’ll be spoiled for options but since we had only 3 pax, we kept it simple and got king crab, abalone, prawns, and the friendly stall lady even added some shellfish for free ☺️☺️☺️
We spent around SGD $300+ for all our seafood (the crab was slightly over 2kg).

After payment, we were led to the 2nd floor restaurants where they cook your seafood the way you like it. We also ordered a few extra dishes there, which came up to about SGD $200 including cooking fees.

Everything was fresh, delicious, and the whole experience was so enjoyable!

Definitely a must-visit spot ☺️

reviews.text:
I am a foreign patient from Australia, and I came to Seoul in February 2026 for breast augmentation. I interviewed three different clinics, and Note PS was my top choice—and the best choice I’ve ever made. This is also the clinic that my travel agent highly recommended. The clinic setting is very laid-back, calming, and professionally set up. The consultants, management team, and in-house translator went above and beyond. Dr Kwon was my surgeon, and he is very skilful at what he does. The fact that he is highly experienced with revision surgery is a bonus, so I can rely on just one surgeon.

Despite this being my first cosmetic surgery, the process was seamless. Recovery for me was much easier than what I had heard others experience. The results looked amazing from day one. I am now almost a month post-op and can do most things easily without any restrictions, and the implants have become much softer. Highly recommend!!!

I chose Note Plastic Surgery through a recommendation from Soomin at Freqty Agency, and I’m very happy with my experience. The entire process was smooth and well-organized, and the staff at the clinic were kind, professional, and attentive.

It has been one month since my procedure, and I’m already pleased with the results. The doctors addressed all my concerns, and I felt supported and well-informed from consultation to aftercare.

I’m grateful to both Note Plastic Surgery and Soomin for guiding me through this journey, and I would confidently recommend them to others.

This was my first plastic surgery and also my first solo trip to South Korea, so choosing the right clinic was really important to me. I’m really glad I chose Note Plastic Surgery.

Dr. Yoo (facial contouring) and Dr. Lee (rhinoplasty + platysmaplasty) were amazing — incredibly skilled, patient, and reassuring throughout the whole process. They really listened to my goals, and gave honest advice

I am now one month post op and very happy with the results so far! The neck/jaw area hasn’t changed much yet, but I know it takes time. The whole team was professional, organised and attentive. I’d definitely recommend Note Plastic Surgery to anyone thinking about facial surgery in Korea.

I was referred to Note Plastic Surgery by a friend, and I’m so glad I chose them for my surgeries. I’ve always been self-conscious about my jawline and nose and wanted a slimmer, more balanced look.

Traveling alone to Korea made me a bit nervous, especially about communicating in a language I’m not fluent in. But the staff and translator were amazing. They made everything easy and stress-free.

Dr. Yoo (Facial Contouring + Zygoma Reduction) and Dr. Lee (Rhinoplasty) really listened to my concerns and gave honest, thoughtful advice about what would suit my face best. They were patient, kind, and explained every step clearly. Even on surgery day, they took time to reassure me and made me feel completely safe.

It’s now been four months since my surgery, and while I’m still healing, I’m happy with how everything is turning out.

Following a friend's recommendation, I chose Note Plastic Surgery for my under-eye fat repositioning (눈밑지방) with fat grafting, and my experience was exceptional.

From the welcoming consultation where the doctor, interpreter, and consultant ensured my goals were met, to the streamlined surgery day, everything was handled with detail and care. Dr. Lee was reassuring and clearly explained the procedure (which involved fat transfer from my side under anesthesia).

The post-surgery care was top-notch. Minseon and Annette were wonderful, thoroughly explaining medications. The team even arranged for pumpkin juice (호박주스) and porridge (죽) to be delivered to my accommodation, and provided transportation to and from the clinic, which was a huge help.

Recovery was just as Dr. Lee predicted: slight puffiness at week one, and by week two or three, my under-eye darkness was gone! I look and feel incredibly refreshed.

I highly recommend Note Plastic Surgery for their professionalism, outstanding care, and amazing results.

Dasan Fortress Library is a district library in Jung-gu that opened in May 2021. The size is a total of three floors, consisting of a literature library on the third floor, a general library on the second floor, a children's library on the first floor, and an outdoor terrace. The library facility itself is very small, but thanks to the unique interior created in a narrow space, you can stay and go in a distant and pleasant way. In addition, we also run a cafe named The Masil Cafe.

The only downside of this library is its accessibility. It is about 600m on foot from the nearest Bertigogae Station, and it has a considerable slope of up-and-down, making it difficult to come to use it from outside unless you are a nearby resident. Still, it's a unique library, so it's worth looking at at at least once.

reviews.text:
Mixture of good to desirable items on wnd floors in half of the proud vendors/ collectors themselves. Then, there are souless seller who put in mass produced knock-off antique repros from China and copycat paintings from South Asia. The latter are the one who will discourage people to come and cobfidently buy authentic Korean heritage pieces.

I don't think I will dig this place much as they are retailers with overpriced retail prices for not superior quality pieces but they have put the popular items in good conditions. Not so much of unique sides. But you will still meet a few genuine collector/ vendors on 2nd floor who you will befriend with during your visit. They share their passion for the antiquity and history of Korea and the neighboring countries that will humble you.

Just stay away from  tourist stores. I just can't believe some crass Korean visitors fall for these tasteless water color or oil paintings from South Asia with fancy modern frames, or, massive granite carvings from China with Korean subjects, that was never authentically Korean scale at any rate. reviews.text:
Pretty interesting Chinatown in Seoul. A lot of Korean Chinese influence including banchan stores, lots of lamb skewers, and north east Chinese food options. It had its unique demographic and Korean-Chinese influence that is different from Japan/Singapore/US Chinatowns. Some people who work here do not even try to talk in Korean, but in Chinese. Good place to get authentic Chinese seasonings and banchan. I’d get produce and seafood from other places.

I had heard a lot about this traditional market, and I finally visited on the first day of the Lunar New Year. I was surprised to see that it was still very crowded, as I had expected most stores in South Korea to be closed for the holiday.

Walking around, I almost felt like I was in China because there were so many shops selling Chinese products and a wide variety of Asian groceries, including durian. The atmosphere was lively and interesting. If you have some time while you’re in Seoul, I definitely recommend checking this market out. I really enjoyed my visit.

A small Chinatown near Daerim station. You can find some Chinese produce and a variety of Chinese food such as Xiao long Bao and La Mian. Overall it is a small place but a pretty great find not far from Seoul.

The biggest Chinese market in Korea.
You can enjoy verious street foods and fresh vegetables.

Do you want to eat Chinese food and speak Mandarin? This is your chance.  This is a major Chinese enclave and this market is liable to make you forget the you're actually in Korea.  This is the first place I've been to where the merchants assume that you're Chinese and start the conversion in Chinese.  Some of them don't even speak Korean.

You know this is real Chinese food because you will be one of the only non Chinese people here.  Almost any ingredient or Chinese staple dish can be found here.

I personally don't speak Chinese but my friend who used to live in China was having a ball.  "I really feel like I'm back in China on this street!" Definitely an interesting twist to the normal  시장 (traditional market).

I'm not so into it,  honestly, but my friend who speaks the language and loves Chinese food said she'd be going back ASAP.

After Korea’s liberation in 1945, this building served as the headquarters for the Ministry of Education and later the Ministry of Culture and Information, becoming the administrative center for national education and cultural policy in the early Republic of Korea.
When those offices moved to Sejong City, the site was reborn in 2012 as the National Museum of Korean Contemporary History.
This makes the museum’s location itself historically meaningful — it’s a place where the modern nation’s governance and cultural identity first took shape.

Inside, the exhibitions are well organized by period, from liberation to the present, making it an excellent introduction to modern Korean history — even for first-time visitors or foreigners.
Its surroundings also add to its significance: right across from Sejong Center and the Government Complex, and just behind it lies Gyeongbokgung Palace and Mt. Bukak. Together they form the symbolic axis of Korea’s politics and history.

One place you absolutely shouldn’t miss is the rooftop observatory on the 8th floor.
From there, you can enjoy a panoramic view of the entire Gyeongbokgung Palace, beautifully framed by the surrounding mountains.
It offers a perfect vantage point to appreciate the geomantic (Pungsu-jiri) harmony of the palace’s location — encircled by mountains that were believed to protect the king and ensure the dynasty’s stability.
It’s not just a museum; it’s a window into Korea’s landscape of power and tradition.

Highly recommended — especially the rooftop view that reveals the deeper meaning of Gyeongbokgung’s setting.

The facilities, including bathrooms, are well-maintained, and the lawns are spotlessly cared for, creating a welcoming environment. I’ve been to the National Theater of Korea a few times now. I watched La Traviata last September, Joyous Resonance in January, and L’italiana in Algeri in February. Each show was different, but they all had that moment when the lights dim, the orchestra begins, and the whole room breathes together. That’s the part I love most.

The theater is one of the biggest in Korea. It went through a renovation in 2021, and it looks great. The halls are clean, the seats are comfortable, and everything feels new. Still, I think a great theater needs more than just a nice building. It needs warmth. It needs to feel like a place made for people, not just for performances.

If you are planning to visit with kids, there is something you should know. Getting there is not easy. The theater sits halfway up Namsan Mountain, right in the middle of Seoul but far from the subway. The nearest station, Dongguk University on Line 3, is not within walking distance. You have to take a bus, usually number 420. Now, imagine yourself holding your child and a bag while standing on a crowded bus on your way to an opera. You will probably be tired before you even get there.

That is why I think accessibility matters. A public theater should welcome people from the moment they decide to come, not make them wonder how to reach it.

Once you are inside, things get better. The space feels open and organized. There are four floors, labeled L, 1, 2, and 3. Each one has vending machines for water and soft drinks. On the L floor, there is a restaurant called Central Yunit. It looks comfortable and has many seats, although it seems a bit expensive. There is also a KB Bank ATM nearby, which is convenient.

The box office is on the 1st floor, which feels like the 2nd floor if you are used to the American floor system. There is a small café that sells sandwiches and coffee, and the box office opens one hour before the show. The staff are calm and polite. You can leave your coat in the cloakroom across from the counter. They put a numbered sticker on the back of your ticket so you can pick it up easily after the show.

There are plenty of seats for intermission, and the atmosphere stays quiet and comfortable. After the performance, shuttle buses take people back to Dongguk University Station and Dongdaemun History and Culture Park Station. If you miss one, another comes in about twenty minutes.

Yes, getting there takes effort, but once you sit down and the music starts, you forget about all of that. The voices rise, the stage glows, and for a while, everything else fades away. That is the beauty of live performance, and it is why I keep coming back.

Daehanmun is the main gate of Deoksugung Palace.
'Daehan' means "Hanyang will prosper."
Hanyang refers to the sunny region north of the Han River and was the old name for Seoul, the capital of the Joseon Dynasty.
'Han' means 'Han River', and 'yang' means 'north of the water' or 'sunny place, reflecting Hanyang's geographical characteristics.

title: Dogok Market

reviews.text: Lively, clean, with a wide variety of prepared goods, fruit, vegetables, and seafood. If you can't find something you want here, you're just not trying.

LNestled in the heart of the city lies a small traditional market that packs a flavorful punch. With approximately 20 shops clustered together, this market offers a vibrant snapshot of Korean culinary traditions.

As you navigate the narrow alleyways, you're immediately enveloped by a tapestry of aromas and sights. The market boasts an impressive array of Korean staples: from the pungent notes of gochujang (red pepper paste) and doenjang (soybean paste) to the briny scents of saeujeot (fermented shrimp) and galchijeot (fermented hairtail fish). The golden hues of chamgireum (sesame oil) and deulgireum (perilla oil) glisten in bottles, promising to add depth to any dish.

Beyond the fermented goods and oils, the market is a treasure trove of fresh produce. An assortment of seafood glistens on ice, while vibrant vegetables add splashes of color to the bustling scene. It's a one-stop-shop for those looking to stock their pantries with authentic Korean ingredients.

However, the market's popularity comes with its challenges. The high foot traffic can make navigation somewhat difficult, especially during peak hours. Shoppers should be prepared for close quarters and the occasional brush with fellow market-goers.

A word of caution: the narrow pathways are sometimes shared with small motorcycles making deliveries. While this adds to the market's lively atmosphere, visitors should remain alert to ensure their safety.

Despite these minor inconveniences, the market remains a must-visit for food enthusiasts and those seeking an authentic Korean shopping experience. The density of shops means you can compare prices and quality easily, ensuring you get the best products for your won.

In conclusion, this compact traditional market offers a concentrated dose of Korean food culture. It's a place where centuries-old culinary traditions meet the hustle and bustle of modern city life. Just remember to watch your step, and you're in for a treat for all your senses.

reviews.text: A lone watch tower which was part of the palace in the past. Now it is at a road intersection.

Dongsipjagak (동십자각) is a small guard pavilion located at the eastern corner of Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul. Built during the Joseon Dynasty, it served as a watchtower and a key point in the palace's defense system. Its unique architecture reflects traditional Korean design and historical significance.

Known as the lonely pavilion, the Dongsipjagak was once part of the palace watch tower is now standing as the center of what seems like a roundabout. There appeared no door to this pavilion but was told of its history dated back to be part of Gyeongbokgung Palace.  I guess must be the new city layout that now stands its current position. So, next time when you pass by this lonely pavilion, give a second look and appreciate its history and its once critical role as a watch tower protecting the Palace.

reviews.text: The D Museum invites the visitor inside -- not just to view some art, but to imagine it in one's own life. The current exhibition sets up scenarios of family members' households at different stages of their lives -- complete with exquisitely designed furniture and modern artwork. It features lesser- and well-known artists, such as Picasso and Frank Lloyd Wright. You might find yourself wanting to sit in that beautiful chair in that beautiful living room to admire the art (or in my case, the curtained dining area on a raised platform surrounded by stones), but please don't as you will be immediately escorted out.

We visited D Museum for the Art is Life, Life is Art exhibition and had a wonderful experience. The curated “houses” were beautifully designed—modern yet deeply rooted in Korean culture. It was inspiring to see such a thoughtful mix of works by Korean, Japanese, Spanish, and Italian artists, alongside big names like Picasso, Frank Lloyd Wright, and Patricia Urquiola.

It’s a fantastic and well-rounded exhibition that we’d definitely recommend to art and design lovers. A helpful side note—there are lockers available and they’re free for the first hour, which made it convenient to explore comfortably. 🖼️🏠🎨✨

We saw the Romantic Days gallery and it was fantastic. It's 3 floors worth of display so admission is definitely worth it. The also have courteous ushers so that visitors are assisted every step of the way. I'd say this place is perfect for dates. They even have photobooths at the lobby so that you can take home a memory of the day.

I visited the D Museum during the Romantic Days exhibition. I recommend this museum as it often changes up their theme and the tickets are afforable if you  book online. The area is also very nice and near Seoul Forest, so perfect for a day out.

I thought D Museum would be slashed off my itinerary, but I'm glad it didn't. I arrived an hour before it closes in the evening, and it was packed with young visitors (which I wasn't surprised about). The "Weather" exhibition is so amusing that it takes you to the sensations of each season, transitioning from one room to another. My favorite must be the collection for winter. This is definitely one of my favorite destinations in my recent Seoul trip, and this particular gallery is one of the most unique I've been to.

reviews.text:

Great way to spend 2 hours with a toddler. The time goes by fast and they're so enthralled by the different play areas that you can take a break too. Plenty of seating for adults to watch / play with their kids on a comfortable surface.

Only downside is how strictly they try to enforce their way of "playing", which means always following the arrows on direction to walk, not climbing while holding any toys, etc. Bro, they're kids. You can get past this by just paying lip service but not relenting to their demands. That's pretty much what I did until they stopped bothering us.

This was the largest kids cafe we visited while in Seoul (we went to several) and my son LOVED it. He ran around everywhere and we also played with him on this digital running game that’s beneath the jungle gym. They have several play stations and my son even loved the lady at one of the stations. However! Something to note! I was in desperate need of a coffee and the cafe was on a break at the exact time we arrived (they take an hour break from 2-3 or 3-4. I like that they have some areas where the parents can sit on the floor as well. We were very comfortable.

This experience honestly still makes me angry and upset.

Last summer, when I was nine years old, my mom and I traveled over an hour by train from my grandma’s house just to come here. I was extremely excited. I had been to the Diki Diki playground before when I was younger, and it was one of my happiest memories. I was waiting for the elevator, full of excitement, thinking I was finally going to play there again.

Then everything fell apart.

I was denied entry because of the age limit, even though I was only ONE year over. One year. For a huge playground where many other places allow kids my age without a problem. That alone was heartbreaking.

But what truly made this experience unbearable was the staff’s behavior.

The employee who stopped us was rude, rolled his eyes, ignored my mom, and treated her with complete disrespect. Watching my mother be treated like that was devastating. She is older than him, a paying visitor, and a parent who spent time, money, and effort just to bring her child somewhere special.

What made it even worse was that the other employees did absolutely nothing. They didn’t step in. They didn’t call a manager. They didn’t try to calm the situation. They just ignored us and continued serving other customers as if nothing was happening, while a child was crying nearby. I felt invisible. Like we didn’t matter at all.

The situation escalated, voices were raised, and I was completely overwhelmed. I was hiding in corners, crying, sitting on the floor, wishing I could disappear. I didn’t even want to be there anymore. My excitement turned into humiliation, fear, and heartbreak within minutes.

That night at dinner, I couldn’t even speak. I shut down completely.

Rules are rules, but there is absolutely no excuse for staff acting this way and for others standing by and ignoring a clearly distressing situation involving a child. This wasn’t just a bad visit. It was an experience that stayed with me and still hurts to think about.

I hope management seriously reflects on how staff behavior and inaction can deeply affect families and children.

reviews.text:
Free museum dedicated to the American columnist Albert Taylor. a figure who played a decisive role to promote the fierce independence movement of Korea and the brutality of Japan on March 1, 1919. I'd love to share my incredibly positive experience at Rovl Avenue for liposuction surgery. From the moment I first contacted them for my consultation, I felt an immediate sense of welcome and ease, which continued throughout my entire journey with them.

The clinic itself is beautifully maintained and exceptionally clean, creating a very reassuring environment. Every single member of the staff I encountered was genuinely kind and pleasant, contributing significantly to a comfortable experience.

A special shout-out goes to Toni, my translator. She was an absolute gem – so kind, patient, and pleasant to interact with. She meticulously answered all of my questions, no matter how many I had, and ensured I understood every detail, which was incredibly helpful.

The doctor, Jung Rae Jun, was equally impressive. He was incredibly thorough in his explanations, detailing every aspect of the procedure and what to expect. What truly set Rovl Avenue apart from other consultations I had was their unwavering focus on safety; I felt that this was a top priority for them, unlike elsewhere. I particularly appreciated their use of an ultrasound to accurately assess the amount of fat, which demonstrated a precise and personalized approach. Dr. Jung Rae Jun also set realistic expectations regarding my results, which I found very reassuring. Throughout the entire process, I felt completely safe and well-cared for.

Beyond the procedure, Rovl Avenue also provided excellent recovery services, ensuring I was comfortable and healing well. They even went the extra mile to make sure I was well enough and prepared for my travel home, which was a huge relief.

Overall, if you're looking into liposuction and want a clinic that emphasizes professionalism, safety, and thorough care, Rovl Avenue is worth considering. I'm very satisfied with my experience and the care I received.

Recently I had thigh lipo in Rovl. From my first online consultation and my first visit everyone in the clinic is very sweet, they explained everything very thoroughly and reassured me. It made me feel very comfortable and at ease from the consultant, front desk personnel to the nurses.

Dr. Kim acknowledged  all my concerns and goal.  Answered every question I had and also I could tell he put patient safety a top priority. Never once did I feel rushed as I did with the other surgeons I had previously visited.

On the day of my surgery, I was very nervous but I knew I was in good hands he explained everything in details told me what I should expect before and after the surgery. He wasn’t over promise and went through all the consequences.

Although I am only 7 days post-op, its still swollen,  and numb in some area. But all the pain is gone and I don’t have much bruises in the back thigh area. I could sleep, walk, squat, sit comfortably. It indicate thats the Doctor was very gentle during the suction procedure.

Thank you so much Rovl Avenue, I appreciate your time and attention in smoothing out my lipo journey.

I recently had arm liposuction at Rovl and I'm really happy with both the results and the overall experience. The staff were kind and made sure I felt comfortable throughout the whole process. They were great about answering all my questions, which really helped ease my nerves.

There is an observation deck on the roof which gives you a decent view of the whole Gimpo airport. Probably worth a visit if you’re headed to the airport anyway.
