reviews.text: After passing Jeongdong Theater along Deoksugung Palace's stone wall road in Jung-gu, Seoul, you'll find a vine-covered red brick building marked as the 'Former Shin-A Ilbo Annex Building.' Built in the 1930s with reinforced concrete, it was originally a private headquarters for an American sewing machine company. The building had one underground and two above-ground floors, with stairs leading to the first floor. Shin-A Ilbo acquired it in 1969, adding two more floors in 1975. Following media consolidation by the military government in the 1980s, it became the Shin-Ah Memorial Hall.

The former Shin-A Ilbo building in Jeong-dong, Jung-gu, Seoul. It was designated as a national registered cultural property on August 27, 2008
It was designated as a national registered cultural property on August 27, 2008. It is a reinforced concrete building built in the 1930s with one basement and two floors above ground. The outer wall was built of red bricks from Shanghai, China. It was expanded to four stories above ground in 1975.

At the end of the Joseon Dynasty, it was used as the office of the Tax General (currently the Customs Service), and the office of German diplomatic advisor Möllendorf was also here. After that, it was used as an office of the Korean branch of the American company Singer Sewing Machine Company and accommodation for its supervisors, and was sold to Shin-A Ilbo in 1963. Since then, the Shin-A Ilbo has been used as an annex to the Shin-A Ilbo until it was absorbed and integrated into the Kyunghyang Newspaper due to the consolidation of media organizations in October 1980.

Along with the turbulent history of the end of the Korean Empire, it is a building of high modern and contemporary historical and cultural value, representing the site of a media disaster in 1980 as a measure to consolidate media organizations of the new military. In addition, it is a reinforced concrete building that was rarely seen in private buildings at the time, and it is a good source for technical history research in modern architecture as it has well-remains architectural methods during the Japanese occupation, such as slab structure and circular reinforcement.
[Dusan Baekgwa]

Shin-A Memorial Hall This place is worth seeing just by building, and on the first floor, you can enjoy light drinks and meals at the cafe.

On the second floor, a gallery specializing in crafts called Contradiction Gallery illuminates the atmosphere here.

reviews.text: My trip started on a high at Sejong Theatre, where I watched the musical Phantom. The performance was absolutely stunning—the set, the music, the voices. For a couple of hours, I was so absorbed I didn’t even check my phone (which, let’s be honest, says a lot for a Gen Z like me). It felt like stepping into a different world, and I left with goosebumps.

My time exploring Sejong Plaza was spent enjoying the beautiful statue of Sejong the Great. There's many animations on the buildings, hidden alley restaurants that are ALL 10/10, and subway/public transportation hub.

The Sejong Center for the Performing Arts is an iconic performance venue located in Gwanghwamun, Seoul. For Korean artists, performing here is considered the ultimate honor, and it wouldn't be an exaggeration to call it the Carnegie Hall of Korea. While the facilities are somewhat dated and inconvenient, they are receiving positive feedback. It is conveniently located right next to Gwanghwamun Square, and it is also great for a walk after the performance. Making its own original performances like Ilmu(One Dance) is also a promising idea.

Exhibition
Masterpieces from the San Diego Museum of Art: "From the Renaissance to Impressionism"

Hey, let me share a quick thought with you.

If you ever find yourself near Gwanghwamun, take a moment to walk by the Sejong Center. And if you already have a ticket in hand, even better. You are about to step into one of Korea’s most meaningful performance halls.

Sejong Center has long been considered a symbol of Korean performing arts. When it opened in 1978, its pipe organ was the largest in Asia. Back in Europe, pipe organs were a way for cities to show their pride and prosperity, and Sejong Center carried that same spirit here in Seoul.

Sure, some people might say it is not the most modern venue anymore. And they would not be completely wrong. But this place holds memories. It has watched generations grow up, quietly standing its ground while the city changed around it. That kind of history matters.

Personally, I have spent some memorable nights here. I watched THE GREATEST: Thrill with Jeong Dong-ha and Sohyang in September 2023, Universal Ballet’s The Nutcracker in December 2023, and Chung Myung-Whun conducting Beethoven’s Ninth with the KBS Symphony at the end of 2025. Since it is a multipurpose hall, you might not always get the same powerful acoustics as a dedicated concert hall, especially for classical music. Still, the experience feels special every time.

Getting there is easy. Just hop on Seoul Subway Line 5 and get off at Gwanghwamun Station. One small thing to note, though. There is no traditional cloakroom. Instead, you will find unmanned lockers on the second floor. They work, but the touch screen can be a little tricky. Maybe it is just me getting older.

The box office is on the first floor, and there are kiosks if you already bought your ticket. You will also spot vending machines for water on each floor, which always comes in handy.

One last tip. The Grand Theater usually opens about two hours before the performance for security reasons, and audiences are allowed into the hall about thirty minutes before the show starts.

Take your time, soak it in, and enjoy the moment.

Visiting the Art Sonje Center in Seoul in Aug 2021 was a profoundly moving experience. The curated space and the photographic artwork were both thought-provoking and evocative. Themes of extremities, natural phenomena, and supernatural beliefs of the locals intertwined seamlessly, each element resonating on different levels. The use of white, thin cotton threads and mummified black lava created a stark contrast, while circles, composition, and texture added layers of meaning that felt both tangible and abstract.

The artwork spoke of redemption, debris, and the fragile linkage—or lineage—between past and present. Half-soaked in salty water, the imagery seemed to evoke the soul of the dead, with brass bowls symbolizing reconciliation rather than perfection. The emotions conveyed were desperate yet hopeful, a delicate balance that kept me reflecting long after I left the gallery.

There were so many elements to contemplate, each knocking on the door of the mind, inviting deeper introspection. The experience was like a conversation with the artwork—ongoing, never quite complete, yet profoundly fulfilling.

I had my revision rhinoplasty with Dr. Choi through Seoul Medical Guide, and I couldn’t be happier with the entire experience. My original nose had very little bridge, and after my previous surgery where the silicone was removed, it became upturned — something that had bothered me for years. These were my main concerns going into the consultation, and Dr. Choi immediately put me at ease.

He patiently explained the process and showed me examples of similar successful results. Dr. Choi reassured me that he could achieve the look I wanted — a higher bridge with a more refined, natural shape. He explained that he would use a silicone implant to create the bridge and donated rib cartilage to define the shape and tip. His professionalism and confidence gave me complete trust in his skills.

The clinic staff were incredibly caring and attentive, always making sure I was comfortable throughout each step. During my recovery, they checked in regularly and provided treatments to support the healing process, which made everything feel much smoother and less stressful.

After years of hesitation and dissatisfaction, I finally have the nose I’ve always wanted. I absolutely love my results — from the elegant high bridge to the cute, defined tip. I’m so thankful to Dr. Choi and the Seoul Medical Guide team for helping me regain my confidence and making this experience so positive and fulfilling.

Appreciate Dr. Choi Min for putting the time and effort into my care. I asked tons of questions during the consultation to make sure I was comfortable enough before progressing to surgery based on what I wanted. He answered most of my questions and made the process as smooth as possible. The surgery itself was surprisingly quick. I didn’t expect all to be done within a couple of hours. Do admit the post op process recovery was rougher than I thought, thought its expected, especially with the bruising. The red light therapy and IV antibiotics helped with the recovery process at each follow up. I also appreciate how attentive the front staff were in welcoming me to the clinic. I am still awaiting my final results, but am overall satisfied with the current outcomes.

So happy I came to this clinic. I traveled from the US here on a strong recommendation and they really put my mind at ease here. Definitely recommend to anyone looking to come here for medical/esthetic procedures.

reviews.text:
I had an excellent experience at Etonne, and I’m really glad I chose this clinic.

From the consultation to post-op care, everything felt thoughtful and professional.  What I appreciated most was that Dr. Cho Jeongmok was very conservative and honest; he didn’t try to upsell unnecessary procedures and clearly explained what would and wouldn’t benefit my face.

The eyelid surgery itself was smooth, and my recovery has been much easier than I anticipated.  Even early on, the results look natural and still very much like me, just brighter and more defined which was exactly what I wanted.

The staff was kind, patient, and reassuring throughout the process, especially on surgery day and during follow-up.  I never felt rushed or pressured, and all my questions were answered clearly.

If you’re looking for a clinic that prioritizes natural results, honesty, and long-term aesthetics, I would absolutely recommend Etonne and Dr. Cho Jeongmok!

My Background
I’m in my mid-20s and from Singapore, and this was my very first plastic surgery experience. I did procedures for my eyes (incisional double eyelid + ptosis correction) and my face (AccuLift). Naturally, I was nervous going into it, but the entire experience turned out to be far smoother and more reassuring than I could have imagined.

About My Surgeon, Dr. Cho Jeong Mok
Dr. Cho performed the entire procedure himself. (I know this because I briefly woke up during the process and heard his voice.) I feel genuinely grateful to have been in such skilled hands. He is highly professional, fluent in English, and truly prioritises what’s best for his patients. He really listens for example, he respected my choice to avoid threads and fillers and he explains everything clearly and concisely without overwhelming me. I felt safe and confident with him from start to finish.

Staff and Translators
As a foreigner, I honestly don’t know how I would have managed in the operating theatre without Milk and Yenni, my translators. They made sure every single word was translated to me while I was lying on the operating table, which made a huge difference. The rest of the team  the anaesthesia staff, managers, and nurses were incredibly gentle, careful and professional especially when injecting/removing my stitches. They made me feel completely at ease throughout the entire process.

Consultation Process
Everything from pre-consultation to post-care was incredibly smooth. The clinic responds promptly, which reassured me at every step. Even the online consultation before my trip gave me a clear idea of the procedure and a ballpark estimate of the cost. Honestly, it didn’t take me long to decide on this clinic,  I had followed an Asian American beauty influencer who recommended Etonne, and I could tell her review wasn’t filtered or sponsored.

Costing and Transparency
Etonne’s pricing is transparent. After my in-person consultation, I was given a fair and clear quote, which made me even more confident in my decision.

Clinic Location and Cleanliness
The clinic is in a prime location in the heart of Gangnam, directly above the subway station, making it very convenient. The space is clean, hygienic, and has a prestigious atmosphere, which gave me confidence even before stepping into the procedure room.

Recovery and Results
My recovery has been fast, and the results are good. I’ve received compliments from friends, family, and even strangers. Now at week two, I still have some mild bruising, which is completely normal. The aftercare kit  including a cooling pack, saline solution, and Q-tips was very helpful, and the vitamin drip after surgery helped me regain energy and clarity quickly.

Final Thoughts
Experience it for yourself. I wrote this review in full confidence and in depth because the entire process genuinely went smoothly. I feel very fortunate that my first plastic surgery experience was with Etonne. The combination of Dr. Cho’s expertise, the professionalism of the team, and the seamless overall process made everything a success. I highly recommend this clinic to anyone looking for skilled, reassuring, and truly professional care.

I originally wanted to do incisional eyelids surgery, but he suggested a less invasive approach and walked me through long term scenarios and think beyond the present moment.I had such a great experience speaking with the doctor that I decided to do chin filler, radio therapy, and Botox all at the same time as well.  I also wanted to do more chin filler but he provided his own opinion and in the end we agreed on more minimal chin filler. I highly recommend my doctor, Dr. Cho Jeongmok. The results for my eyelids and chin/jawline looks amazing thanks to him.

I’m from the U.S., and this was my first time having any procedures done in Korea. I consulted with several clinics via WhatsApp, but Etonne stood out for being responsive, clear, and thorough, which led me to cancel my other consultations and book with them.

The clinic was clean and modern, and the staff were very kind and professional. During my consultation, Dr. Kim Jaegon spoke perfect English and took a conservative approach, recommending a non-incisional upper bleph and a slight alar reduction instead of the more extensive procedures I initially requested. His honesty and lack of pushy sales made me feel immediately comfortable and trusting.

My surgery went smooth, and post-op care was great. Although it’s been less than two weeks and my results are still settling in, I’m very happy so far. I’m especially grateful for Dr. Kim’s judgment in knowing exactly what was enough to achieve a natural yet enhanced result. I highly recommend Etonne and have already referred all my friends.

Chloe helped me through the entire process and was very responsive over WhatsApp. Dr Kim speaks English well and my consultation with him gave me a lot of confidence that I would have a natural result. They were able to share before and after photos of other Caucasian patients (with their permission) during the consultation which was so helpful and encouraging. The experience at the clinic was very professional and caring. I highly recommend Etonne and Dr Kim.

title: Walking along the Saetgang River in Yeouido
google_addr: 4-9 Yeouido-dong, Yeongdeungpo District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: I didn’t know this place existed until I came to the nearby park. I decided to take a walk through it, which took me a little over an hour. I stopped to take some quick photos along the way before heading back. I think this place will be really beautiful in the spring.

Saetgang Ecological Park, located in Yeouido, Seoul, is a place where you can take a quiet walk and feel nature away from your busy daily life. It is easily accessible by public transportation as it is within walking distance from Exit 2 of Singil Station. This park was established in 1997 as the first ecological park in Korea, and was built with the goal of preserving the natural ecosystem. One of the biggest features of Saetgang Ecological Park is its various natural ecological facilities. There is a 1.2 km (0.75 miles) long waterway, where you can enjoy the harmony of water flow and ecosystem. Aquatic plants grow around the waterway, and you can observe aquatic plants and small creatures living there. A 6 km (3.73 miles) walking trail circles the entire park, and as you walk along the path, you will experience various ecological environments.

Yeouido Saetgang Ecological Park is centered around Saetgang Stream, a tributary of the Han River, and features a wide variety of flora and fauna, making it a haven for nature enthusiasts. It is particularly impressive for its wetlands, which are home to migratory birds, amphibians, and rare plant species. The well-maintained trails and wooden boardwalks meander through lush greenery, providing visitors with a peaceful environment to unwind, jog, or cycle. The elevated observation decks scattered throughout the park allow for panoramic views of the wetlands and the Seoul skyline, creating an ideal spot for photography and birdwatching.

Yeouido Saetgang Ecological Park is both an exciting and relaxing place to visit. It is exciting because it has a beautiful bridge connecting two busy roads and some meters above the forested park. At the same time, it is relaxing because of the green forest and nature… It is also great for hiking.

We thoroughly enjoyed walking in this green space on the edge of the busy financial district.
Nice wide paths, lots of coverage from the sun, and plenty of benches to sit and relax.

Yeouido Park covers approximately 230,000 square meters (2,475,700 Square feet).
The park is divided into a traditional Korean forest, a lawn, a cultural yard (Munhwa Madang), and an ecological forest.
The cultural yard and the bike paths throughout the park are remnants of the Yeouido Plaza era.
Due to its location in Yeouido, it serves as a park and resting place for both office workers and visitors. Surrounding the park are several buildings, including the Yeouido Financial District.

Yeouido Park stands as a pinnacle of creativity and aesthetics, seamlessly blending nature with thoughtful design.

Walking around its serene pathways offers an unmatched sense of calm and relaxation. The lush green spaces and tranquil water bodies create a peaceful escape from the everyday rush.

Divided into diverse sections, the park captivates visitors with its unique features, such as the picturesque grassy pond, the enchanting traditional Korean forest, and the eco-rich ecological forest.

Each area invites exploration, making it a perfect sanctuary for those seeking both beauty and tranquility.

reviews.text: Yeouido Hangang Park is a wonderful place to relax and enjoy beautiful riverside scenery. The wide open spaces, well-maintained paths, and fresh breeze make it a perfect spot for walking, cycling, or simply sitting down and enjoying the view. The atmosphere is calm yet lively, especially during sunset when the sky becomes really beautiful. It’s a great place to hang out with friends or family while taking a peaceful break from the busy city.

Wide open space, a large park beside the Han river that has its own bicycle lanes for slow and fast riders. Great for runners and walk-marathoners alike. The views are fine between the Seongsan and Hangang Railroad bridges. You can see in the distance the Namsan tower behind the cityscape. Tip: go here during the early morning and exercise; go when there are decors, or events especially with light shows.

Yeouido sits by the Han River and is one of three public parks that makes up Hangang Park. This park is accessible by the Seoul Metro and serves as the place where you can ride on a river boat for a cruise. During winter, a snow sled area gets set up from mid December to February

I like that it's a strip of Riverside. Overlooking the other part of Seoul. Cooling breeze with chairs for public to sit and enjoy. .. I saw many people picnic there as well. There are some floating shops there... CU Ramyeun library.... Can eat superb noodles Riverside!

I visited Yeouido Hangang Park at night, and surprisingly it didn’t feel as “Instagrammable” as I had expected. The area was quite quiet during my visit, possibly because of the cold weather, so the atmosphere felt a bit empty.

Still, the riverside view at night has its own charm, but overall it may be better to visit during warmer seasons or earlier in the day when the park is livelier.

Yeongdeungpo District is a dynamic and diverse area in southwestern Seoul, South Korea. Known as a commercial and business hub, it is home to a mix of residential, retail, and industrial spaces. Yeongdeungpo is a key part of Seoul’s economic landscape, with major office buildings, shopping centers, and the Yeongdeungpo Times Square, one of the largest shopping malls in the city. This mall offers everything from fashion and electronics to a variety of restaurants, entertainment options, and a large cinema.

Despite its modern, bustling atmosphere, Yeongdeungpo also has areas of greenery, such as Yeongdeungpo Park, where locals come to relax and enjoy outdoor activities. The district is also home to a number of traditional markets, like Mokdong Market, where visitors can experience authentic Korean food and street vendors.

Yeongdeungpo’s central location provides excellent transportation connections, with multiple subway lines and bus routes passing through, making it easy to access from other parts of Seoul. The area has a diverse population, with both young professionals and families calling it home, and it offers a lively combination of modern urban living and traditional Korean culture.

When I visit South Korea, I always make it a point to explore traditional markets. Perhaps it's the nostalgia of the bustling rural markets during my childhood or the distinct aroma of a vibrant market, but there's something special about these places that I always look forward to. However, my recent visit to Yeongdeungpo Market left me with a sense of disappointment.

The market, known for its declining business, felt truly disheartening. It's a stark contrast to the popular and lively traditional markets you often find in South Korea, where both locals and foreigners gather to enjoy the variety of food and other attractions. In contrast, Yeongdeungpo Market was so quiet that it seemed like there were more staff members than customers. The overall atmosphere felt rather sluggish, which was unexpected.

Perhaps the less-than-ideal image of a traditional market in other places, with its charm and untidiness, was perceived quite differently here. The dark and somewhat dreary atmosphere made it appear untidy to the point of surprise. This visit was a reminder of how traditional markets can differ greatly in their vibrancy and appeal. I'd rate my experience at Yeongdeungpo Market with 2 stars.

title: Seoul Arts Center
google_addr: 2406 Nambusunhwan-ro, Seocho District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text:
I remember that afternoon so clearly—I was riding the metro through Seoul, feeling the gentle sway of the train as we moved from one neighborhood to the next. It was one of those unplanned moments of a vacation that turned into something special. There, amid the ads for local teas and tech gadgets, was a poster for the Renoir-Cézanne exhibit at the Seoul Arts Center. I'd always loved Impressionism from afar, flipping through books on rainy days back home, but seeing these names in person, in a city so full of its own vibrant energy, felt like an invitation I couldn't ignore.
I made my way there on a quiet weekday, hoping for a peaceful visit. What I found instead was a room full of people, all drawn to the same quiet thrill. It surprised me how many others had the same idea, even on a Tuesday. A kind staff member at the entrance noticed my hesitation and explained they were managing the flow to keep things comfortable. She gave me a slip with a time slot, just twenty minutes away. That wait didn't feel like a delay at all; it gave me time to sit nearby, watch families and friends share excited whispers, and enjoy a simple cup of coffee from the café. By the time my turn came, I was eager, my mind already wandering to what lay ahead.
Walking in, I was struck by how alive the paintings felt. Renoir's soft, warm scenes of people in gardens and city streets pulled me right into their world—the way the light seemed to dance on the canvas made me pause and just breathe it in. I'd read about Cézanne's mountains and still lifes before, but standing there, tracing the steady lines of his brush, it was as if he was showing me how to look at a hillside or a simple fruit in a new way. For someone seeing these works for the first time, it was quite an experience, like sharing a quiet conversation with old friends I'd only known through stories.
And then, near the end, the rooms opened into Picasso's pieces—a shift from gentle impressions to sharp, thoughtful forms that caught me off guard in the best way. His bold colors and shapes felt like a bridge to something more urgent and alive, rounding out the afternoon with an unexpected depth. I stayed longer than I meant to, letting the soft light from the gallery windows fall across the floors as I moved slowly from one wall to the next. Too bad photography wasn't allowed, but I'm so thankful I made the trip.

title: Former Yongsan Seminary and Wonhyo-ro Jesus Sacred Heart Cathedral

reviews.text: Very good

The Yongsan Sacred Heart Seminary (formerly Yongsan Seminary Sacred Heart Cathedral), which is now part of the Sacred Heart Girls' High School Correctional Center, and the former Yonghan Seminary building, which is used as an office and a memorial hall for the Sacred Heart Sisters, still retain the traces of the time when it was a nail in the sanctuary.

Located in Wonhyo-ro 4-ga, Yongsan-gu, Seoul, the former Yongsan Seminary Cathedral was built in 1902. This is where the remains of Saint Kim Dae-gun Andrea, a priest who was the first room of the Korean Catholic Church, were enshrined from the time of construction to 1958, and the remains of Bishop Sobrugier, the first diocese of Joseon, and Bishop Mutel, the eighth diocese, passed through.

Korea's first seminary finds its origin in a seminary established in Baron, Chungcheong-do in 1855. Prior to that, efforts to cultivate Korean clergy had already begun in the 1830s, and in 1836, Kim Dae-gun, Choi Yang-up, and Choi Bang-je were given theology education in Macau.

Barron Seminary was closed in 1866 due to the persecution of the sick, but as freedom of faith was secured, 21 people were sent to Penang Seminary in 1882 as international students. In 1885, Jesus Sacred Heart Seminary opened in Beomgol, Gangcheon-myeon, Yeoju-gun, Gyeonggi-do, and in 1887, it was relocated to Yongsan, Seoul. In 1892, a new seminary teacher was built, and the cathedral was built and constructed as a cathedral affiliated with the seminary in 1902, 10 years later. Yongsan Seminary Cathedral was designated and preserved as Historic Site No. 255 with the teacher in 1982.

After that, several seminary schools, including St. Justino Seminary in 1914 and Deokwon Seminary in Hamgyeongnam-do in 1927, followed by Seoul, Daegu, Gwangju, Busan, Suwon, and Daejeon, and Incheon Catholic University opened in 1996.

The former Yongsan Jesus Sacred Heart Seminary. Currently, it is used as a memorial hall for the Sacred Heart and as a nun's office.Bishop Sobrugier, the first diocese of Joseon, whose remains were enshrined in the former Yongsan Seminary Cathedral, was appointed the first diocese president when the diocese of Joseon gained independence from Beijing in 1831. However, he overcame various hardships and diseases and tried to enter Joseon land, but eventually died at the age of 43 four years after leaving for Joseon in front of him.

Although he did not enter Joseon, the Korean church became a completely organized church as Father Imitation and Father Shastang soon entered Joseon along the route of entry he pioneered.

Archbishop Mutel, the 8th diocese of Joseon, a member of the Paris Outer School Association, entered Korea in 1877 and spent his entire life working in Korea, a foreign land, except for a few years in the middle until he died in Seoul in 1933.

Bishop Mutel, who was active during the persecution era, built Jesus Sacred Heart Seminary, Jonghyun Cathedral, and Yakhyeon Cathedral to further solidify the appearance of the church liberated from the underground church after the Treaty of Korea-France, while providing much support for the creation of the main hall in each province.

The exterior of the former Yongsan Jesus Sacred Heart Seminary Cathedral.Above all, however, his greatest achievements can be attributed to the martyr Hyunyang, the establishment of the Catholic Church in Korea, and the beatification of the martyrs. The famous Mutel diary was written from August 4, 1890, when he was appointed as the head of the Joseon Diocese, to December 31, 1932, just before his death, and recorded the personal situation of the bishop and the church during his tenure with a total of 6,000 pages, which is a valuable material for our Korean church.

In addition, he wrote "Mutel Document" and "Geohae Diary" and when the original white paper of Hwang Sa-young was discovered, it was translated into French and distributed to academia, and the original was consecrated to Pope Pius XI at the beatification ceremony of the 79th Korean martyr in 1925. Currently, the white paper Hwang Sa-young is housed and displayed at the Missionary Folk Museum in the Vatican Museums.

The former Yongsan Seminary Cathedral is where the remains of many martyrs were laid. The remains of eight former Joseon dioceses, including St. Kim Dae-gun, Korea's first priest, Bishop Brugier, the first bishop of the Joseon Diocese, St. Angbert, the second bishop, the third bishop of Pereol, the fourth bishop of St. Vernon, the fifth bishop of St. Davlue, the sixth bishop of Liddell, the seventh bishop of Blanc, the eighth bishop and Bishop Mutel, who presided over the dedication of the cathedral, were all laid in the cathedral. The remains of the martyrs laid here were then moved to Hyehwa-dong Seminary Cathedral, Myeong-dong Bishop's Cathedral, and Jeoldusan Martyr's Holy Land, while the remains of previous dioceses were moved to Yongsan Clergy Cemetery and buried. In 2010, repair work was carried out on the exterior wall and surrounding of the aging cathedral, and in 2011, repair work is underway on the interior of the cathedral. [Source: Jupyeongguk, from heaven to earth - Following their fragrant footprints, Catholic Publishing Co., 1996; Partial modification and addition of content (Final modification, February 19, 2020)]

Wonhyo-ro Jesus Sacred Heart Cathedral purchased a site with a view of the site of Saenamteo and Danggogae Martyrs in 1887 and built it as an affiliated cathedral of Jesus Sacred Heart School, the predecessor of Catholic Theological Seminary in 1902.
After the Catholic University moved to Hyehwa-dong, it is used as an annex to Seongsim Girls' Middle and High School.
The building next to the cathedral, which is currently being used as the Sacred Heart Memorial Hall, was used as a seminary and was built in 1911.
The beautiful Gothic cathedral and seminary buildings, like Myeongdong Cathedral, were designed by Father Coste of the Paris Outline Church and are privately designated.
The cathedral is located inside the girls' school, so it may be difficult to enter on weekdays.

It is located inside Sungsim Girls' Middle and High School. So if you want to go on weekdays, you have to enter through the security office at the main gate, but you may not be able to enter without your ID. The cathedral itself was very mysterious and beautiful.

A very good place for walking, relieving stress, and reflecting. The park is not large, but it is located on a hill, so you can get some cardio exercise while enjoying the smell and view of the forest. The very convenient paths laid out around the perimeter of the park and numerous benches make the park an excellent place for walking. And the rest areas with wooden tables and chairs allow you to sit down for a snack or a chat. It is very important that all the wooden paths are equipped with illuminated railings, so you can walk even in the dark. At first, I didn't understand why the paths in the park had such gentle slopes and inclines until I saw a sign indicating people with limited mobility. Yes, even people in wheelchairs can move around the park.
The park has some very unusual areas, as if for overcoming obstacles, where small pebbles alternate with wooden planks and then with large stones. There is also a toilet in the park, which is very clean and comfortable.

Nice barefoot path, they also had balance beams, workout equipment, kids playing dodgeball, lots of small birds singing, and I think I saw a couple of racoon-dogs running in the woods. Nice view from the top.
Not sure if it's a destination for travelers, but I would love to live next to a park like this.

The Olympics were held in Seoul in 1988. Of course, a lot has changed in the city since then. But the beautiful Olympic Park remains, with all its sports infrastructure, which still serves the Korean people. For me personally, the Olympic Park has become a wonderful place for walks and relaxation. You can simply stroll leisurely along the alleys or go for a run. There are plenty of benches for resting, toilets, and vending machines on the grounds, so relax among the shady trees and recharge your batteries.🙏
There is a very unusual service in the park. If you have walked a lot and your feet are tired, you can use a special foot bath with cool water to relieve fatigue, which is very cool.👌
The coffee shop in front of the park is quite expensive. Vibe in the morning is quite good. On weekdays, the subway is very crowded.

Olympic Park (올림픽공원) is a must-visit spot in Seoul if you're looking to enjoy nature, art, and a bit of history all in one place. The park is massive, with wide walking paths, scenic lakes, and open green spaces that make it perfect for a relaxing stroll or picnic.

All around the park, you’ll find large-scale sculptures and public art that add a unique charm to the landscape. There’s also historical significance here, with remnants from the 1988 Seoul Olympics adding character and depth to the visit.

Whether you’re into photography, jogging, or just need a peaceful break from the city buzz, Olympic Park offers a refreshing escape with something for everyone.

It is a sacred place where martyrs are honored as an internationally recognized holy place of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Seoul

The shrine of Waegogae Pass is where the Korean Armed Forces Central Cathedral, which is the seat of the bishop of the Gunjong Diocese, is currently located.

Yongmun Market in Yongsan is a traditional neighborhood market just a few minutes’ walk from Hyochang Park Station (Line 6 / Gyeongui–Jungang). It’s not a flashy tourist spot – it’s where local residents actually shop for meat, seafood, vegetables and side dishes, and recently the market has been renovated so the alleys are brighter and easier to walk through.

If you’re tired of tourist traps and want a more down-to-earth place to eat, Yongmun Market is a great option. Prices are generally reasonable, portions are generous, and most shops are clearly focused on regulars, not one-time tourists.

Some food spots worth checking out in and around the market:

Changseongok (창성옥) – A classic haejangguk (hangover soup) institution with decades of history. The broth is deep and rich, filled with beef bone flavor, ugeoji (greens) and soft blood curd. Many locals order a fried egg on the side and mix it in. It’s hearty, old-school Korean comfort food and perfect on a cold or rainy day.

Yongmun Haejangguk (용문해장국) – Another legendary place, often mentioned as one of the “big 3” haejangguk spots in Yongmun area. In the morning, they basically serve only haejangguk, with a very simple, focused menu, then switch to beef-bone dishes and stews in the evening. The soup is strong, the kimchi and radish pickles are excellent, and the overall feel is very local.

Janggun Bossam (장군보쌈) – A famous bossam (boiled pork with kimchi) restaurant near the market, known for its soft pork slices, fresh napa kimchi and, in season, oyster bossam. It’s been featured on Korean TV and is always busy with locals coming for dinner, group meals and drinks.

Vision Mandu (비전만두) – A small stall at the entrance side of the market selling old-school snacks like hot dogs, croquettes and chapsal donuts at very friendly prices. Everything is fried to order, hot and crispy, and the taste feels like classic Korean street food from years ago. The owner is known for being kind and chatty with customers.

On top of these, you’ll find many small banchan shops, fruit stalls with surprisingly cheap prices, butcher shops and seafood stands. It’s the kind of place where you can eat a proper meal, grab some snacks to go, and also feel how a real Seoul neighborhood market works – without constantly worrying about being overcharged.

If you want a more local, relaxed and honest traditional market in Seoul, Yongmun Market is a very good alternative to the more touristy places. Come hungry, walk slowly through the alleys, and just follow the lines of local people – that’s usually where the best food is.

title: Mount Yongma

reviews.text:
I’ve hiked over 25 mountains in the greater Seoul area, reaching every summit, so I can confidently say that Achasan (아차산) is one of my favorite rocky mountains. What sets it apart is the stunning viewpoints along the trail—not just at the top like many other hikes. The climb is relatively short too—about 45 to 50 minutes to the summit, even with a few leisurely stops to take in the views or sip some coffee.

That’s exactly why I keep coming back on weekends.

From this rocky ridge, you get panoramic views of Seoul in all directions. On a clear day, you can see far into the north, south, and east. But honestly, no photo or video can truly capture the beauty of this mountain and the breathtaking scenery it offers.

There are several trail entrances, but I personally love starting from the 어울림정원 (Eoullim Garden) entrance. The trail from there climbs steeply—almost a 45-degree rocky path—leading up to 팔각정 (Palgakjeong Pavilion). Along the way, there are multiple scenic spots, so make sure to pause, look back, and take in the views around you—not just what’s ahead.

Beautiful Mountain range between Seoul and Guri-si. You can visit many temples and fortress in this mountain. View of Hangang River and the bridges. You will need about 3 to 3.5 hrs to complete the mountains of Achasan and the mountain on the north (forgot the name of it)

Compared to many popular mountains in Seoul like Bukhansan or Dobongsan, Achasan can be viewed as a piece of cake in terms of the level of difficulty and time required. There are a few access points and I accessed it via (...). I made it to the Goguryeojeong pavilion in 10 minutes and reached the Achasan peak in just shy of an hour. The hike comprises of a combination of wooden stairs, rocks and dirt trails. It's fairly easy without challenges of steep steps. There are a few picturesque lookouts along the way so be sure to stop and snap a few photos. The peak, however, is rather disappointing because it's just a stone plaque that tells the height of the mountain without any breathtaking views of the type that you usually get on mountain peaks. As the signage marking the peak is diminutive and easy to miss, many people stop there to take a photo of the signage as proof of hiking to the peak  From Achasan you can access Yongma-san, another mountain located less than 2 kilometers away. The interesting part of the hike was the presence of Goguryeo dynasty-era forts, especially how they remained in tact from the Gorguryeo dynasty until the 1990s when historical excavation works took place. An interesting part of Achasan's history. If you hike beyond the peak towards Yongmasan, you will come across the third and fourth forts shortly. The forts are closed to public viewing so don't expect to see any historical relics on display, but rather just signage explaining the history of the fort and the items excavated. Overall, a good hiking trail for beginners. Parking is a huge problem here though. I ended up parking in the market area, which is about a 10 minute walk away but you can use the chance to discover the endless number of Korean eateries that line the street that leads to the access points to the mountain.

reviews.text: My trip started on a high at Sejong Theatre, where I watched the musical Phantom. The performance was absolutely stunning—the set, the music, the voices. For a couple of hours, I was so absorbed I didn’t even check my phone (which, let’s be honest, says a lot for a Gen Z like me). It felt like stepping into a different world, and I left with goosebumps.

My time exploring Sejong Plaza was spent enjoying the beautiful statue of Sejong the Great. There's many animations on the buildings, hidden alley restaurants that are ALL 10/10, and subway/public transportation hub.

The Sejong Center for the Performing Arts is an iconic performance venue located in Gwanghwamun, Seoul. For Korean artists, performing here is considered the ultimate honor, and it wouldn't be an exaggeration to call it the Carnegie Hall of Korea. While the facilities are somewhat dated and inconvenient, they are receiving positive feedback. It is conveniently located right next to Gwanghwamun Square, and it is also great for a walk after the performance. Making its own original performances like Ilmu(One Dance) is also a promising idea.

Exhibition
Masterpieces from the San Diego Museum of Art: "From the Renaissance to Impressionism"

Hey, let me share a quick thought with you.

If you ever find yourself near Gwanghwamun, take a moment to walk by the Sejong Center. And if you already have a ticket in hand, even better. You are about to step into one of Korea’s most meaningful performance halls.

Sejong Center has long been considered a symbol of Korean performing arts. When it opened in 1978, its pipe organ was the largest in Asia. Back in Europe, pipe organs were a way for cities to show their pride and prosperity, and Sejong Center carried that same spirit here in Seoul.

Sure, some people might say it is not the most modern venue anymore. And they would not be completely wrong. But this place holds memories. It has watched generations grow up, quietly standing its ground while the city changed around it. That kind of history matters.

Personally, I have spent some memorable nights here. I watched THE GREATEST: Thrill with Jeong Dong-ha and Sohyang in September 2023, Universal Ballet’s The Nutcracker in December 2023, and Chung Myung-Whun conducting Beethoven’s Ninth with the KBS Symphony at the end of 2025. Since it is a multipurpose hall, you might not always get the same powerful acoustics as a dedicated concert hall, especially for classical music. Still, the experience feels special every time.

Getting there is easy. Just hop on Seoul Subway Line 5 and get off at Gwanghwamun Station. One small thing to note, though. There is no traditional cloakroom. Instead, you will find unmanned lockers on the second floor. They work, but the touch screen can be a little tricky. Maybe it is just me getting older.

The box office is on the first floor, and there are kiosks if you already bought your ticket. You will also spot vending machines for water on each floor, which always comes in handy.

One last tip. The Grand Theater usually opens about two hours before the performance for security reasons, and audiences are allowed into the hall about thirty minutes before the show starts.

Take your time, soak it in, and enjoy the moment.

reviews.text: This place is absolutely amazing!! Worth the trek in every way. Wonderful museum. 90% is outdoors, so visit when the skies are clear!

My best day ever
U guys must visit here
You can not go there by walk

Good starting place to learn something about Korea stone sculptures, or at least know culturally what the stone sculptures are used for.  After a brief tour, now I knew a bit about Muninseok, Beoksu and Dongja sculptures.  Out of the museum building, there were more sculptures in the garden.  A lot to see.
The museum has also worked with Google Map to enable anyone to 'street view' the exhibits in their garden as they wish to expose the museum to more people locally and overseas.
It is also interesting to learn how the museum was started.  It was started by a successful businessman (also the Chairman of the museum) who is nationalistic and determined to keep Korean stone sculptures which some are national assets from being taken out of the country.  He also managed to buy back some from overseas collectors and bring them back home.  This museum is newly relocated from the old one.  He has chosen Seoul, perhaps more metropolitan - having potentially larger audience, both local and tourists, to expose the cultural stories behind all these stone sculptures.

title: Stamp Museum
google_addr: 70 Sogong-ro, Jung District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: Passed by the Post Tower while exploring Jung-gu during the Lunar New Year holidays. We wanted to visit the Museum inside, but unfortunately it was closed. The location is convenient if you’re sightseeing around the area, but do check the opening days if visiting during public holidays.

The Stamp Museum was a fun and unique place to visit. We loved the stamps you can collect as you walk around the museum. There are plenty of postcards and other small items you can take as souvenirs which made the visit even more enjoyable. There are videos and other interactive pieces that share interesting history and there are archives you can pull out from drawers to look at stamps from different time periods. The fact that the museum is free to enter is amazing.

For the negatives there is not much English translation inside the museum as most of the information is only in Korean. It can also be a bit hard to find within the building. I do not think there were toilets on site although they might be in another part of the building. It also feels like the museum is aimed more toward children than adults.

Overall it is a charming and educational stop especially if you enjoy collecting or looking at stamps.

Visited the museum to buy stamps but ended up being told nothing was available or rather all sold out.
The museum is very child friendly and I shall get my kids along for my next South Korea trip.
I asked around and wasn't directed to any counter but straight to a shop located outside the building, where I did manage to get many stamps especially BTS stamps.

The Korean Postage Stamp Museum is located in the basement of the Seoul Central Post Office building. Being on my second visit, the museum has changed since my first visit in mid 2019. It has become more interactive and child-friendly. Entry is free and there are free lockers to store your possessions until the 5pm closing time.

However, the museum counter no longer sells commemorative back issues of Korean stamps as it used to. This is a great pity as one of the joys of visiting the museum previously was to purchase stamps (especially important for stamp collectors) at face value - who would say no to a presentation folder of the 2018 North-South Summit as a nice keepsake!

To purchase commemorative stamps, head to Counter 10 of the Central Post Office, which is connected through a linkway to the museum, and ask for "special stamps". Stamp selections are mostly miniature sheets and far more limited in variety - but can still be bought at face value
Interesting museum of stamps and post right in the middle of Myeongdong. Many stamps and figurines from not just Korea but around the world. It's free as well.

An Unforgettable Escape: My Heartfelt Review of Walkerhill Hotels & Resorts, Seoul (5/5)
Stepping into Walkerhill Hotels & Resorts in Seoul was like entering a dream. From the moment I arrived, I felt an immediate sense of peace and luxury that truly melted away all the stresses of travel. This wasn't just a hotel stay; it was an experience that touched my heart and left me feeling utterly refreshed.

What truly sets Walkerhill apart, for me, is its breathtaking location. Perched atop a hill, surrounded by the lush Acha Mountain and overlooking the majestic Han River, the views are simply unparalleled. Waking up to the sunrise painting the sky over the river, or seeing the city lights twinkle below at night, was a daily moment of awe. It felt like a secluded oasis, yet I knew the vibrant energy of Seoul was still easily accessible thanks to their convenient shuttle service.

Beyond the stunning scenery, it was the genuine warmth and attentiveness of the staff that truly made my stay exceptional. Every single interaction, from check-in to dining, was met with genuine smiles and a desire to make me feel welcome. They anticipated my needs before I even voiced them, and their kindness felt truly sincere. It's rare to encounter such consistent, heartfelt hospitality, and it made a huge difference to my overall feeling of well-being.

My room was a sanctuary of comfort and elegance. Spacious, impeccably clean, and thoughtfully designed, it offered everything I could wish for and more. The bed was incredibly comfortable – I slept like a baby! And the view from my window, whether of the mountain or the river, was a constant reminder of the beauty surrounding me.

I also thoroughly enjoyed the various facilities. The pools, both indoor and outdoor, were fantastic for a relaxing swim, and the surrounding green spaces were perfect for a leisurely stroll. There's a wonderful sense of tranquility throughout the entire complex.

Leaving Walkerhill Hotels & Resorts, I felt a genuine pang of sadness. It was more than just a place to sleep; it was a place where I felt truly cared for, where I could unwind completely, and where I created beautiful memories. If you're looking for an escape that combines stunning natural beauty, impeccable service, and a truly luxurious experience in Seoul, look no further. Walkerhill has captured my heart, and I already dream of my return.

He deftly handles interesting twists and turns and did a great job of motivating all of us to follow suit.  Another nice plus is that Taejin snapped numerous photos of all of us along the way.  Soon after the tour was over, he sent them out to the group in a convenient Google Photo Album (no extra charge).  He has a nice quality camera so the photos are all very high quality.  We definitely recommend this tour.  It is a great way to learn about Seoul and have a lot of fun along the way.

We booked an afternoon e-bike tour for two, and Hagar was our guide. The tour was informative and moved at a good pace. Hagar had a great personality — easy to talk to and knowledgeable — and shared a lot about the history and culture of Seoul.

We rode through different neighborhoods, each with its own character, and learned about the city’s past from its early history to modern times. The e-bikes made it easy to get around without feeling rushed or tired.

It was a good way to see more of the city and understand it beyond the usual tourist areas. I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a different way to explore Seoul.

The bike bus is an excellent option to tour around Seoul, especially on your first visit. The guides take you to some off beaten track places and share some great fun stories along the way. The atmosphere was fabulous and chill throughout the tour. 🤩🤩

reviews.text: Good place to remind this poet

The site of the boarding house where Yoon Dong-ju, a poet of unlucky genius, stayed.
When the poet entered Yeonhui Technical School (now Yonsei University) in 1938, he lodged in the school dormitory, Bukhyeon-dong, and Seosomun area, and it is said that he lived in Nusang-dong 9 in Jongno-gu from May to September 1941.

It is the home of novelist Kim Song, who was usually admired by the poet, and stayed for only five months, but since the boarding house wrote ten poems such as "Star Counting Night" and "Self-Portrait," it is remembered as a meaningful space today and visitors are constantly visiting.

In fact, at the time of poet Yoon Dong-ju's stay, it was a tile hanok, but now its old appearance has disappeared and only a sign saying "Yoon Dong-ju boarding house" is attached to the wall of a multi-family house. About 180 meters from the boarding house, you will find the Suseong-dong Valley, the entrance to Inwangsan Mountain.
Jeong Byung-wook, a professor at Seoul National University who was the poet's friend and roommate at the time, recalled this period, "Before breakfast, I took a walk to the middle of Inwangsan Mountain in the mountain behind Nusang-dong, washed my face anywhere in the mountain valley, returned to my room, finished cleaning, and went to school after breakfast."
It is a unique attraction that attracts people to see what inspired young poet Yoon Dong-ju, who Koreans love. (Korea Tourism Organization). Every corner of Korea)

Eunpyeong Historical Hanok Museum is an absolute gem for anyone interested in Korean culture, architecture, and history. Located right next to the beautiful Eunpyeong Hanok Village, it’s the perfect place to start your visit if you want to understand the deeper meaning behind traditional hanok design and the lifestyle it represents.

The museum is not very large, but it’s incredibly well curated. The permanent exhibition shows the evolution of hanok architecture — from structure and materials to cultural symbolism — and explains how traditional homes were adapted to Korea’s seasons and way of life. Even without speaking Korean, it’s easy to follow thanks to clear visuals, models, and English explanations.

The building itself is impressive — a modern interpretation of hanok architecture with wide wooden beams, open spaces, and beautiful natural light. There’s a calm, respectful atmosphere that makes you want to slow down and really take it all in.

Staff are friendly and helpful, and entry is either free or very affordable. It’s rarely crowded, so you can enjoy the exhibits peacefully. Don’t miss the rooftop terrace — it offers a lovely view of the surrounding village and Bukhansan Mountain.

This museum is a must-visit if you’re already in Eunpyeong Hanok Village. It helps you see the traditional houses around you with completely new eyes. Highly recommended for anyone who loves culture, architecture, or just quiet, meaningful places in Seoul.

Itaewon Market: A Global Bazaar in the Heart of Seoul
Itaewon Market, a vibrant stretch in Seoul's cosmopolitan district, is a microcosm of the world's cultures. It's a feast for the senses, where the aromas of exotic spices mingle with the sounds of diverse languages.
The market's narrow alleys are lined with shops overflowing with treasures from around the globe. Here, you can find Turkish carpets, Moroccan leather goods, Indian textiles, and African handicrafts. The antique stores are a haven for collectors, offering vintage cameras, vinyl records, and other nostalgic items.
Food lovers will find themselves in paradise. The market boasts a plethora of international restaurants and street food vendors. Sample savory Turkish kebabs, spicy Thai curries, authentic Italian pasta, or crispy Korean fried chicken. Don't forget to try the local specialty, Itaewon tacos, a fusion of Mexican and Korean flavors.
Beyond shopping and dining, Itaewon Market offers a glimpse into the neighborhood's rich history and multicultural identity. The area is home to a mosque, a historic church, and a variety of cultural institutions.
Whether you're a seasoned traveler or a curious local, Itaewon Market is a must-visit destination. It's a place to explore, discover, and immerse yourself in the world's diverse cultures without leaving Seoul.

Tucked away in the bustling heart of Seoul, the Ilmin Museum of Art offers a small but richly rewarding experience for visitors interested in contemporary Korean art. Although the museum occupies a modest space, its well-curated exhibitions provide a thoughtful exploration of various artistic expressions.

Upon entering, I was immediately struck by the museum's commitment to showcasing innovative Korean artists. Each exhibit, meticulously arranged and presented, invites viewers to engage deeply with the themes. The museum excels in creating an intimate atmosphere where each piece of art can be appreciated in its own right.

A standout feature of the museum is the cinema room located on the top floor. This unique space offers a series of thought-provoking films that delve into the struggles of modern Korea. The films, ranging from documentary to experimental, challenge viewers to reflect on socio-political issues that shape contemporary Korean society. It's a poignant reminder of the power of art to influence and reflect cultural and historical narratives.

The museum also benefits from its dynamic location. Situated near Gwanghwamun Square, it provides easy access for anyone looking to immerse themselves in Korea's rich historical and cultural tapestry after visiting the museum.

Overall, the Ilmin Museum of Art is a compelling destination for those who seek to understand the pulse of modern Korean art and its reflections on society. While the space may be smaller than some of its counterparts, its exhibitions are thoughtfully selected and profoundly impactful, offering fresh perspectives on significant issues. I left with a deeper appreciation for the role of art in societal discourse and would recommend a visit to anyone with an interest in contemporary art and cultural reflection.

reviews.text:
ILCHI ART HALL is tucked away on the second basement floor of the King Kong building. Outside, you cannot miss the awkward King Kong statue hanging off the building. The box office is just near the main entrance.

To be honest, I had a hard time finding the entrance myself. It is surprisingly small, so I even took a picture to help others recognize it more easily.

The hall has about 220 seats, which makes it a fairly intimate venue. I think it works well for small events. I personally enjoyed Utagokoro Rie’s concert there on February 22, 2025.

About the seating, each section is marked by letters A, B, C, D, E and so on. Each lettered section actually has two rows, divided by yellow steel bars. The catch is that both rows in the same letter share the same elevation. This means you should always try to book the front row of that pair for a clear view.

For example, seats D-07 and D-27 are at the same height. If you sit at D-07, you will enjoy the performance without obstruction. But if you end up in D-27, you will be staring at the back of someone’s head the whole time. In that case, even E-07 is a much better choice. Trust me on this.

It’s a vibrant shopping and entertainment destination in downtown Seoul that offers a variety of options for visitors. Spanning 11 impressive floors, the mall is thoughtfully divided into sections: Fashion, Living, and Culture. It features the I Park Department Store, Digital Shopping Center, and Event Park, with standout attractions such as a CGV cinema, e-Sports Stadium, miniature golf, and a large bookstore. With over 100 restaurants, a diverse food court, and charming cafes, the dining options are plentiful. Shoppers can explore an array of electronics, fashion, and home goods, while cultural events, fashion shows, and festivals add to the lively atmosphere. Additional features like a video game arcade, an outdoor garden, and a culture center makes it a good destination for shopping, dining, and entertainment in the city!

I'Park Mall is a huge shopping mall at Yongsan Train Station, with many clothing shops and anime-related stuff (pop mart, Studio Ghibli, Marvel, toys, Nintendo Switch, etc.) and an arcade and lots of gacha. But no, I will recommend any tourists to spend half a day here if you're nearby. There are many things to do here!

It's connected to Yongsan Station, where the blue subway line 1 and many Korean trains depart. title: Museum of War and Women's Human Rights
google_addr: 20 World Cup buk-ro 11-gil, Mapo-gu, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: This is an essential visit. I do not remember the last time I was so moved by a museum. The courage, solidarity and strength of the halmoni’s in the face of their tremendous suffering is deeply palpable in each exhibit and learning this history of these survivors especially in the face of continued global erasure and denial feels like a small act one can take to end violence against women. I am so grateful this museum exists, may these women and their descendants, may we all, may the world know peace.

This museum and the personal stories that were told brought me to tears. This museum is incredibly powerful.

Even as a Dutch person from Indonesian parents, I'm aware of the term 'comfort women'. But I've never heard personal stories. I can't imagine what these women has been going through, because there's no word to describe something as cruel as that.

We came from Japan yesterday where we have visited several WWII related sites. Living in a Dutch city that was severely damaged by bombing during WWII, I wanted to learn more about the Japanese part of this story. Of course, as expected, Japan doesn't acknowledge their role and their crimes during WWII. We travelled to more countries and we've learned about their war crimes. Like the death mars in Borneo for example. And the terrible camps in Thailand. But none of those areas taught us about this part that involved women.

We have a profound respect for the surviving ladies who are making a difference by demonstrating every Wednesday in front of the Japanese embassy. It's a disgrace Japan still doesn't acknowledge the facts and choose to ignore it.

Visiting this museum makes you more aware of these war crimes and how women and girls have suffered and are still suffering worldwide. It has to stop. These brave Korean women are still fighting for recognition. But visiting this museum, you show support and that's the least you can do.

Other than that, this museum is small. But the exhibitions are impressive and they hit you hard. We've spend 2 hours in the museum. The audio tour is included in the fee. The audio has an English option and it really gives you an experience filled with emotions, rather than just telling facts. The entrance is subtle and can be easily missed, by the way.

We highly recommend visiting this museum.

I can't describe how intense this museum is. All the memories and experiences are so moving and important. If you get the chance, come here and listen to this part of history that we should remember, always.

This museum was very educational and impactful. While at times it was a bit confronting its message was beautiful and necessary.

It was easy to find using Naver although keep in mind there are several staircases inside the museum and I’m unsure if there are ways around them. However it did have an audio guide available in multiple languages including English which was surprising and good quality.

This is a great place to learn more about the violence Korean women faced under the Japanese soldiers and women around the world continue to face as well as to pay your respects and donate if you can. I even saw a woman bring her daughter and son which I thought was a good idea to increase awareness and understanding among the younger generations.

Definitely worth checking out if you have time!!

A wonderful museum experience. The museum is in a quiet location and seems unassuming from the outside, but the amount of information, media and exhibiting objects they displayed was very impressive. I learned so much not only about history but also human suffering, resilience and hope.

I went when the Kim Bok Dong special exhibition was on, and it was such a special experience that made me tear up several times. The museum did an excellent job depicting her as a wonderful, exceptionally strong woman who despite her own suffering reached out to victims in need.

I also really appreciated the English audio guide devices the museum kindly provided, as I did not speak Korean at all but was still able to learn so much from the museum. This is an unforgettable experience, would definitely recommend it to others.

Jungmyeongjeon Hall, located at the end of the alley on the right side where the Jeongdong Theater ends at the entrance of Jeongdong-gil, is also worth a tour. Jungmyeongjeon Hall is the place where the Eulsa Protectorate Treaty was forcibly signed on November 17, 1905, when the Korean Empire was surrounded by the Japanese military and deprived of diplomatic rights. Inside, the conference room attended by eight ministers of the Korean Empire, including Hirobumi Ito, a key figure at the time of the signing of the Eulsa Protectorate Treaty, and Lee Wan-yong, a representative pro-Japanese party. In addition, materials related to the Hague envoy dispatched by King Gojong to announce the invalidity of the Eulsa Treaty are on display. OH – The Fourth Stand-in for the Dictator
Jeongdong Theater, Seoul

When comedy falls silent
The Jeongdong Theater’s OH – The Fourth Stand-in for the Dictator feels less like a traditional musical and more like a staged narrative with music. On a modest rectangular stage, a skilled live band with cello, piano, and winds provides the strongest moments of the evening. Vocals, however, prove uneven: a deep, resonant baritone appears only once, while much of the remaining singing feels thin and high-pitched.

Visually, the production makes inventive use of descending set pieces and a playful puppet sequence, though such ideas appear too rarely. The story of a supermarket worker turned reporter under a dictator is told consistently, but the leads lack charisma. Comedic touches go largely unacknowledged by the audience, leaving the tone subdued.

At more than two hours, the show maintains interest thanks to its music and stagecraft. As a musical, though, OH never fully convinces.

Jogyesa Temple is a beautiful and peaceful spot right in the middle of the city.

The vibrant lanterns, ancient trees, and traditional temple buildings create a calming atmosphere despite the busy surroundings.

It’s a great place to pause, reflect and experience a bit of Korean Buddhist culture.

The voice of the temple's abbot chanting sutras, amidst the resonant drumbeats, penetrates deep into the heart.
This marvelous combination of sound waves in the listener's soul. During the festival, the temple is beautifully decorated, and I saw Dragon claw Chrysanthemums here, which I hadn't seen in years. The flowers were so huge and stunning! Every morning, the temple holds its rituals, and the sound of chanting carries far into the distance.

Jogyesa Temple (조계사) is a peaceful and uplifting escape right in the heart of Seoul. The moment you step inside, the noise of the city fades and you’re surrounded by calm, colorful lanterns, and beautifully detailed temple architecture. The main hall is stunning—filled with vibrant artwork, golden Buddha statues, and a serene atmosphere that makes you want to pause and reflect.

The temple grounds are impeccably maintained, and the centuries-old trees add a special sense of history and spiritual grounding. Whether you visit during a regular day or during a festival, the experience is always inspiring.

The monks and volunteers are welcoming and respectful, and the signs around the temple make it easy for visitors to understand the traditions and significance of the space. It’s a perfect place for anyone looking to experience Korean Buddhism, take peaceful photos, or simply enjoy a quiet moment in the middle of the city.

A must-visit cultural and spiritual landmark—beautiful, calming, and truly memorable.

It is a traditional Korean cultural space located at the foot of Inwangsan Mountain in Buam-dong, Jongno-gu, Seoul, in the former Anpyeong-gun residence. It is a place where various cultural and artistic programs such as experience, exhibition, performance, and grand hall are operated in four buildings, including the main body and the annex. Especially noteworthy is "Mongyudowondo" painted by Angyeon during the Joseon Dynasty. Mongyudowondo is a masterpiece completed in three days by Angyeon, who told the artist Angyeon that Prince Anpyeong, the third son of King Sejong, saw Mureungdowon in his dream.
This traditional Korean cultural space, located at the foot of Inwangsan Mountain in Buam-dong, Jongno-gu, Seoul, is housed in the former residence of Prince Anpyeong. A variety of cultural and artistic programs, including hands-on experiences, exhibitions, performances, and rentals, are offered across four buildings, including the main building and annexes. A particular highlight is the Joseon Dynasty-era painting "Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land." This masterpiece, completed in just three days, reflects a dream Prince Anpyeong, the third son of King Sejong, had dreamed of, and told the artist about it.

The place where Anpyeongdaegun's utopia was born as Angyon's Mongyudowondo.  It is said that Ojinam Hermitage in Jongno was moved as it was and the beautiful hanok was recreated.  The parking lot is convenient and it is a good place to look around in a quiet hanok.

It is a traditional cultural space located in Buam-dong, Jongno-gu. Originally, it was a hanok building in Ikseon-dong, and it is said that the calligraphy at the end of the Joseon Dynasty was the home of Lee Byung-jik, and it was the place where the 7.4 inter-Korean joint statement was drawn. It is said that it was operated as Ojinam, a restaurant, and was built as a hanok cultural space in its current location using the building materials. The current location is famous for making Angyeon draw Mongyudowondo, and there is a corner where copies of Mongyudowondo are displayed and explained in detail in a small room. Even if it is not an exhibition, it seems to be a special space where you can feel the beauty of Hanok.

title: Cha Min-sung Medical Clinic

reviews.text:
I got a top up of lip filler (last done 2024 in a US clinic) and some facial balancing (cheek filler) done at chamin plastic surgery in Korea. I had a tough time sifting through all the reviews and recommendations on a lot of different platforms, and I found this clinic on Babitok (which is one of the popular platforms I was told locals use). I wanted to write a review because I wish I had something like this to go off of while I was totally overstimulated and paralyzed from the sheer amount of options available lol. I looked at all the before and afters and picked this one cos a lot of the pictures weren’t heavily filtered so you can see the results immediately post and also how it settles in a few weeks later. People also stated how the actual doctor does the consultation himself even tho it’s just for filler - a lot of factory clinics in Korea will have assistants do the consultation so this was different and one of the selling points.

Had a consultation with the doctor on the 6th floor (which is where you will check in as well) The doctor was so kind but also straight to the point; I told him what I wanted and he was able to give me more realistic expectations about the results - and he said he will try to meet my requests as much as anatomically possible. Moved to the 5th floor for the treatment. Sat in a comfy couch in semi private waiting area while waiting for the numbing cream to take effect. Went to the treatment room and completed the treatments with doctor - he took a lot of care and time molding/ looking at the before pics. I got 1cc in lips and 2cc in my left cheek to fix my asymmetry. Pain was a normal level from what you’d expect at these treatments, lessening as you go by. Also they give you a shot of antibiotics/a prescription to fill at a pharmacy.

Overall a great experience, staff was nice too and I’d recommend the doctor because he was very very kind and doesn’t rush you. Staff was also very patient with my questions.

title: Changgyeonggung Palace

~ throw back to mid of November 2025 ~

This palace is so beautiful!

This place is absolutely breathtaking. The scenery stretches out in a mesmerizing panorama, filled with vibrant colors and textures. Lush greenery surrounds the area, and the air feels crisp and refreshing. Sunlight filters gently through the leaves, casting dappled shadows that dance along the ground. Every corner seems alive with natural beauty, from the soft whisper of the breeze to the distant sound of birdsong. It is a place where time feels as if it slows down, inviting you to pause, breathe deeply, and take in every detail of its serene charm.

This palace is connected to the neighboring palace, but you need to buy a ticket to enter each one.
You can either purchase a combined ticket for both places or buy separate tickets at each gate.

I visited early on a Saturday morning after it snowed, and the scenery was stunning. It was a bit cold walking around outside, but I really enjoyed the experience.

Saw this place close to the hotel.   Very large area so lots of walking.   Interesting to read the history, the kings and queens.  Can't imagine the servants going up and down the large stone steps.   Also recognized many areas that have been shown in historical k dramas.   Just loved the architectural designs.   It's winter now so very cold to walk through but minimal crowds.  Able to take pictures without people in the middle of them.  Loved not having to deal with large crowds.

Changgyeonggung Palace is a very pleasant and calming place to visit.

When I went, it was surprisingly quiet, which made the experience even more enjoyable.
The peaceful atmosphere allowed me to take my time walking around and really appreciate the surroundings.

One of the highlights was the garden at the back of the palace which it added to the sense of tranquility and felt like a perfect escape from the busy city.

Overall, it’s a lovely spot to relax, enjoy some greenery and experience a more serene side of Seoul.

reviews.text:
The Joseon Dynasty did not truly come to an end in 1910. It only became history in 1989, with the passing of Princess Deokhye. From the moment thirteen-year-old Princess Deokhye was sent to Japan in 1925 and endured years of suffering, to remaining confined there even after Japan’s defeat, and finally being allowed to return to Korea only when she was nearly fifty and already mentally broken — her life was marked by sorrow at every turn. She then spent the rest of her days quietly living in the land where she was born, until her death. Even simply reading these historical records is enough to leave one choked with emotion.

Although history has passed and today we advocate peace — and cannot hate or forgive on behalf of others — the people who were swept up by the tides of history, those who endured immense suffering and relentless torment, never truly received a sincere apology. And this is true not only for Korea, which was invaded, but for countless people across many nations who endured similar pain.

reviews.text:
An impressive 17-metre-tall statue standing proudly along Gwanghwamun Square. The monument feels powerful & dignified, fitting for the Korea’s legendary naval hero.

At the front of the pedestal are two stone drums & a replica of the famous turtle-shaped battleship (Geobukseon). The Myeongnyang Splash Fountain was turned off during our visit — likely due to the winter season — but the statue remains striking even without the water features.

A significant landmark that’s hard to miss when exploring central Seoul.

This is a statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin at Gwanghwamun Square. It's opposite the statue of King Sejong the great. The front of the statue has multiple fountains but it's not always on so tourists can get near the statue at certain hours.

Yi Su -Sin was a Korean admiral and military general known for his victories against the Japanese navy during the Imjin War in the Joseon period. He fought in at least 23 naval battles, achieving victory in all. In many of these engagements, he commanded forces that were outnumbered and poorly supplied.

One of South Korea's most famous generals!

Very good - this is a statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin and is located opposite the statue of King Sejong the great. The front of the statue has multiple fountains - which are on / off at various hours of the day.

World's greatest admiral, according to both the greatest English and Japanese admirals of all time. There are historical plaques around the statue that you can read up on, plus there are QR codes you can scan to get thorough history lessons. Underneath the admiral statue is a model of tortoise ship that he utilized in defense during his time. There are plenty of water fountains you can jump into, especially those hot and humid summer, and act like a kid 😊 Highly recommend a visit. 😎👍

The BtheB exhibition is basically a beauty exhibition but on a whole different level.
It’s not just about looking at products, it’s about discovering yourself through technology.
What makes this exhibition stand out is the use of MinART technology, a combination of AR and AI that creates a futuristic and highly personalized experience 🤍

Skin & Scalp Analysis
In this area, visitors can check their skin and scalp conditions in detail.
The analysis is powered by AI, making the results more accurate and tailored to each individual.
It feels like a professional consultation, but faster, smarter, and more modern.

Personality Color Test
One of the most exciting parts of the exhibition.
Using AR technology, visitors can discover their personality color, not just based on appearance, but also on vibe, mood, and overall impression.
It’s surprisingly insightful and makes you reflect on how you present yourself.

Decoration & Atmosphere
The decoration is honestly stunning.
Every zone is thoughtfully designed with a clean, modern, and immersive concept.
Walking through the exhibition feels like stepping into a beauty-tech art space rather than a regular expo.

Overall Impression
BtheB successfully blends beauty, art, and technology into one seamless experience.
With the support of MinART, the exhibition feels innovative, interactive, and deeply personal, making it not just visually pleasing, but also meaningful.
