title: COEX Aquarium
google_addr: 513 Yeongdong-daero, Gangnam District, Seoul, South Korea

reviews.text: Pretty good aquarium experience, with a clear path to follow. Kids enjoyed the mermaid show even though it was in Korean. The other exhibits and tanks were also very enjoyable and informative. However, it's not cheap though,and can get crowded, like it's was when we visited on a Saturday afternoon.

SEA LIFE at COEX is such a fun and fascinating place to visit, especially for kids! There are so many kinds of colorful fish and marine animals to see, all beautifully displayed in well-designed tanks.

The aquarium is clean, well-organized, and easy to explore. It’s conveniently located inside COEX Mall, so getting there by public transport is very easy.
Kids and even Adults absolutely loved every moment. A great place for families to enjoy and learn together!

South Korea's premier marine theme parks, located within the Starfield COEX Mall in the Gangnam District. It is home to over 20,000 marine animals representing 650 species, spread across 14 themed zones under the theme "Fantastic Journey of Water."

Opening (2000): Originally opened as the COEX Aquarium, it was the first marine theme park in Korea to introduce professional concepts like "aquarist" and structured marine storytelling.

Acquisition (2022): The facility was acquired by Merlin Entertainments, a global leader in location-based entertainment, as part of their strategy to establish flagship attractions in major gateway cities.

Rebranding (2025): On July 26, 2025, it officially rebranded as SEA LIFE COEX, Seoul Aquarium. This transition included a major "glow-up" with updated branding, improved animal habitats, and new interactive exhibits.

Ocean Kingdom: Features South Korea's largest shark habitat, housing 17 different species including the sand tiger shark.

Deep Blue Sea Tunnel: An immersive walkway where visitors can observe sharks and rays swimming directly overhead.

Seal Beach Cove: A newly expanded area for harbor seals that is five times larger than the previous habitat to better reflect their natural land-based behaviors.

Unique Experiences: Offers Seoul's first glass-bottom boat ride over shark enclosures and a "Sea at Night" zone that uses media art to enhance the jellyfish exhibits.

a reproduction textbook for public buildings

The post office is an exhibition space that is far from commercial characteristics of remodeling a building that was used as a post office into an exhibition space.
While the exterior still retains the general characteristics of the post office building, the interior has been regenerated close to white space, but the interior facilities and traces that were used as a local branch of the post office are still in place.
In particular, the large vault remaining inside and the 30-centimeter-thick vault door are thought to be unique to this space.
The second floor is renovated to be a seminar room, and there are facilities to handle group meetings.
Outside the first floor, there was a fireplace for destroying official documents and a small chimney used as a shredder at the old post office, so I felt the sense of the times that it must have been a post office that was used before the 1990s.
Although the space is not large, it is a wonderful place that reflects regional characteristics as a cultural space while maintaining individuality in the region.

This is a space that is maintained at private expense, not at city or public expense. (as has been the case with most alternative spaces)
It is located inside the alley, and there is no parking space. It is not a space that has a universal character as a family outing location. The exhibition changes every month, not a permanent exhibition, so you need to search for the exhibition through a web search and refer to it.

reviews.text: Jongmyo Shrine is a quiet and spiritual sanctuary right in the middle of busy Seoul. I love how well they have preserved the traditions here. I highly recommend taking the free guided tour, which is available in both Korean and English. it takes a little over an hour and provides great context. While the buildings themselves aren't flashy or tall, the immense scale of the space and the simple architecture are truly amazing. A must visit for a peaceful break and a deep dive into Korean history!

Jongmyo Shrine is the oldest Confucian shrine in Seoul.
And the most authentic of all.
It is located in the downtown (as far as I understood when I was there).

Originally, the shrine was built in the 14th century and it keeps its current form since the 16th century.

When you enter it, there is a path that you are not allowed to walk on - this is a path for spirits... As you enter the territory of the park, you pass by several buildings, all of which are built in accordance with traditional pungsu principles (simplifying it, balancing the key elements, as well as balancing the human life with the elements).

It is one of the key sites that you should visit if you are in Seoul.
It is very peaceful there and I always had a chance to ponder on eternal matters. A perfect place for that...

Jongmyo Shrine is an important historical landmark. It is the ancestry resting place for the tablets of the Joseon Kings and other important figures. The place is smaller than the other 3 palaces, Gyeongbukgung, Changdeokgung and Changyeonggung. Located just outside of Jongno 3 Sam-ga station and close by to Seosulla-gil with its trendy cafes and restaurants. Close on every Wednesday.

Recommend visiting here if you are into visiting historical landmarks or of significance. Joseon Dynasty’s shrine for royal family, it is well maintained, preserved, and shows the height of Confucianism in Korea.

The main attraction/building of the shrine (Jeongjeon) finished its 5 year repair and maintenance work, so it is now fully open and there are no scaffolds barring entry. Good time to visit now.

Tip: If your schedule allows while visiting, I recommend visiting here on the last Wednesday of the month, as entry fee is waived and you can walk around the site freely and tour around at your pace (on regular days, you have to pay to enter and be on a scheduled tour that a guide leads you through).

An excellent place in Seoul to see the ancient heritage of Korea - so we'll preserved.

The shrine is situated on sprawling grounds with thousands of trees with well laid out trails leading the visitors from one building to the next.

In popular belief - the middle stone "median" is not meant for humans to walk on since it is believed that spirits of ancient royalty walk there.

This heritage site deserves a good couple of hours. A very peaceful experience.

Entry is 1000 Won - from the ticket booth located to the outside right of the main gate.

I’ve been to many museums and art galleries and this one was one of the most unique and educational one by far. The exhibit about starting business and how to communicate with people was amazing. reviews.text:
HiKR Ground is a really fun and modern spot to explore Korean culture, especially if you’re into K-pop, K-dramas, and Korean media.

The space is very interactive, with digital installations, photo zones, and hands-on experiences. It’s easy to spend time taking photos and trying out the activities, even if you’re not a hardcore K-pop fan. Everything is well designed and visually impressive.

It’s also free to enter, which makes it a great stop if you’re in the area or looking for something fun to do indoors. The location is convenient and easy to find.

Overall, a great place for tourists and anyone curious about modern Korean culture. Definitely worth a visit if you’re in Seoul.

HiKR Ground is a fantastic experience. It is interactive and completely hands-on, with activities ranging from K-Pop performances/ Karoke,  becoming a DJ, to taking photos and seeing them memorialized on a magazine cover. Kids can explore experiences tied to space, the subway system, and even Korean laundry culture. It is an incredible interactive opportunity for children, and best of all, it is completely free. With 4 to 5 floors of engaging activities, kids will stay busy for hours. We had an absolute blast and highly recommend it.

5 levels of stuff to explore, great for escaping lousy weather. Kids enjoyed the more interactive and visual exhibits. I would have loved for more time to appreciate the artsy and thought provoking exhibits. Free of charge, not crowded on a Thursday noon.

Amazing place not just for kids but adults can fulfill their inner child here too. Free entrance to so many fun things! Even free photo studio area? (something like that) + the whole places looks like straight out of kpop music video. Definitely worth it visiting this place.

Free entrance for you to experience South Korean cultures. There are few floor to explore. Top floor being showcasing the beauty scene of South Korea in photos, then other lower floors have many Kpop experience which teens and kids enjoy. Many photo or video opportunities inside.

title: Hakdoam (Seoul)

reviews.text:
Nice place to visit and see for an hour or so.
Got the car to near the top. Nice statue overlooking Seoul, a temple to relax in, and the mountain with the rock carving.
All very interesting.
Nice to see the sun set over the city.

It is a temple near Bulamsan Dulle-gil, which can be reached after passing a little uphill. You can enjoy a panoramic view of Seoul and the scenery of the mountain, and you can eat bottled water (1,000 won) or a simple snack at the temple entrance cafe. If you are a Buddhist, you can make a wish to the Buddha on the stone wall or put your back on it

It is a small temple located at the foot of Bulamsan Mountain, and the statue of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva carved on a large rock wall is worth seeing.
A high stone wall at the entrance of the temple blocks the view, making it difficult to see the view of the temple. There is a need for improvement.
Close to the city and short hiking time. There is a tea house in the temple, so you can drink coffee while looking at the nice scenery
There is a statue of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, which was created as the owner of Empress Myeongseong during King Gojong's reign in the late Joseon Dynasty.

title: Film Festival under the Han River Bridge

reviews.text: Yeouido Hangang Park is a wonderful place to relax and enjoy beautiful riverside scenery. The wide open spaces, well-maintained paths, and fresh breeze make it a perfect spot for walking, cycling, or simply sitting down and enjoying the view. The atmosphere is calm yet lively, especially during sunset when the sky becomes really beautiful. It’s a great place to hang out with friends or family while taking a peaceful break from the busy city.

Wide open space, a large park beside the Han river that has its own bicycle lanes for slow and fast riders. Great for runners and walk-marathoners alike. The views are fine between the Seongsan and Hangang Railroad bridges. You can see in the distance the Namsan tower behind the cityscape. Tip: go here during the early morning and exercise; go when there are decors, or events especially with light shows.

Yeouido sits by the Han River and is one of three public parks that makes up Hangang Park. This park is accessible by the Seoul Metro and serves as the place where you can ride on a river boat for a cruise. During winter, a snow sled area gets set up from mid December to February

I like that it's a strip of Riverside. Overlooking the other part of Seoul. Cooling breeze with chairs for public to sit and enjoy. .. I saw many people picnic there as well. There are some floating shops there... CU Ramyeun library.... Can eat superb noodles Riverside!

I visited Yeouido Hangang Park at night, and surprisingly it didn’t feel as “Instagrammable” as I had expected. The area was quite quiet during my visit, possibly because of the cold weather, so the atmosphere felt a bit empty.

Still, the riverside view at night has its own charm, but overall it may be better to visit during warmer seasons or earlier in the day when the park is livelier.

reviews.text: One of the most famous and must-do experiences when visiting Seoul, Korea, is taking a trip along the Han River. You can enjoy the stunning views all along the river, and I especially recommend going at night when the scenery is even more breathtaking. The cruise offers live music, which was excellent, and the atmosphere on board is truly amazing.

The cruise 🚢 experience was great, it was perfectly on time. I wish it would have been for a lil longer, it was only for 30 minutes and the time flew by so fast witnessing the beauty of the Han River 🥰🥰🥰

such a surreal experience!! i enjoyed every second of the e-land sunset cruise! seagulls may follow because of dried fish, which you can purchase downstairs in the cu on the cruise and feed it to them. reviews.text:
I wasn’t always a fan of Han River swimming pools—in fact, I had avoided them for a while. The ones I visited in previous years didn’t leave a great impression: the water wasn’t very clean, and some even had an unpleasant odor. But my recent visit to the newly opened pool right next to the Starbucks at Seoul Wave Center completely changed my mind.

I initially went to the area to visit the Starbucks branch, which offers stunning riverside views, and was pleasantly surprised to discover the new pool just next door. Unlike my past experiences, this one was clean, well-maintained, and smelled fresh. The poolside offers a beautiful, unobstructed view of 강북, and the atmosphere felt much more elevated than I expected.

I rented a sunbed for just 10,000 won, which was worth it for the comfort and view. The entrance fee is only 5,000 won, making it an affordable way to cool off and relax by the river. In fact, I’d confidently say the view from here is even better than the one at the more expensive Walkerhill Hotel pool.

The only downside is the limited food options. Since outside food isn’t allowed unless you packed it from home, you’re mostly stuck with typical Korean street snacks like 라면, 떡볶이, 오뎅, and corn dogs—which aren’t really my thing. Also, drinks are only allowed in tumblers, so I’d recommend stopping by the Starbucks beforehand to grab your favorite beverage to enjoy poolside.

Overall, it’s a great summer escape with a surprising level of comfort and a view that’s hard to beat for the price.

Overall, it’s a solid option if you want to switch it up from attending one of the hotel pools in Seoul.

The English guided tour lasted about an hour, though short but pretty intensive.

Though some may think the entrance fee is high, it's worth it, well curated and lots of information like the design of various types of cabinets, tables, book-cases, etc. After which could get close to the furniture and observe the craftsmanship.

An interesting section was the lady's quarter where it displayed and described how a Joseon Queen was dressed with her 6-layer costume before putting on the heavy head-gear. As the Lady mostly stayed indoor,  her room would get the best view and with a large window looking out.  The guide would invite the guests to sit on the floor and experience the scenery (as what the Lady in past did).

Please note no photography is allowed inside the museum.  Around the compound, the guide did not insist.

The Korea National Folk Museum is a beautifully curated place that gives you a real window into how Korean life evolved through the centuries. One of the first pieces that stood out was a stunning driftwood animal sculpture — simple, artistic, and a perfect introduction to the museum’s blend of creativity and history.

Inside, the exhibits walk you through traditional tools, farming equipment, fishing gear, and everyday household items in a way that’s easy to follow and visually engaging. The old handwritten manuscripts and medical texts were fascinating to see up close, showing just how carefully knowledge and culture were recorded and preserved.

The outdoor area adds even more charm. The pagoda is absolutely striking, and the small wooden home replica gives you a quiet moment to imagine how families lived generations ago.

Overall, this museum offers a calm, meaningful experience that deepens your understanding of Korean culture. It’s informative, relaxing, and definitely worth adding to your Seoul itinerary.

reviews.text: Seoul Central Mosque, located in Itaewon, is the largest and most well-known mosque in South Korea. The mosque serves as a central place of worship and community for Muslims in Seoul. Surrounded by halal restaurants and international shops, it also reflects the multicultural atmosphere of Itaewon.

The Seoul Central Mosque (Korean: 서울중앙성원; Arabic: مسجد سول المركزي) is a mosque opened in 1976 in Itaewon, Seoul, South Korea. It is located in Hannam-dong, Yongsan District. It holds lectures in English, Arabic, and Korean. Friday prayers regularly attract between four hundred and five hundred worshipers in the afternoon, though regular attendance has sometimes been known to climb as high as eight hundred people.

Seoul Central Mosque is a peaceful and inspiring landmark in the heart of the city. Blending beautiful Islamic architecture with the vibrant spirit of Seoul, it offers a calm refuge for prayer, reflection, and cultural connection. The welcoming atmosphere, diverse community, and spiritual serenity make it a must-visit place for anyone seeking tranquility and unity beyond borders.

reviews.text: This is the place where the 3rd King Taejong Yi Bang-won and Queen Wongyeong were buried.

Heonneung is a twin tomb of King Taejong of the 3rd Joseon Dynasty and Queen Wonkyung of the Yuan Dynasty. From the time of its construction, the right side was left empty and planned to be a Ssangneung tomb, and the two tombs were connected into one with a railing stone. It is the first Ssangneung tomb since the foundation of the Joseon Dynasty, and the number of gates and unmanned people deployed to the top of the tomb is twice as large as other tombs. When Inneung Royal Tomb of Soonjo was built in 1856, it was called Heoninneung Royal Tomb.
When Queen Wonkyung ascended in July 1420, it was located in the south of Daemosan Mountain in Gwangju-gun. On September 17, it was commissioned and called Neungho Heonneung. When King Taejong ascended in 1422, on September 6, the palace was placed in a stone chamber and placed as Ssangneung.
- In 1446, Yeongneung was built as a joint tomb between Sejong and Empress Sohyeon on the west side of Heonneung, but it was moved to Yeoju in 1469.

Seoul's Hidden Cultural Jewel, White Wave Art Center

Hello, cultural explorers! Today, I would like to introduce you to a beautiful complex cultural space located in Seocho-gu, Seoul, and the White Wave Art Center. Located in the middle of the legal complex, this place feels like a wave of art washes away the starkness of the city.

The Birth of the White Wave Art Center
The White Wave Art Center began with a lawyer's beautiful dream. It was created with the desire to plant the seeds of culture in the cold atmosphere of the legal complex and to spread the purity and goodness of the people like a wave. Opened in 2007, it has since become the cultural center of Seocho-gu.

a variety of cultural spaces
The White Wave Art Center is not just a concert hall, but a complex cultural space. There are three performance halls, galleries, publishers, and bookstores.
= White Wave White Hall: 457-seat Main Concert Hall
= White Wave Art Theater: 303-seat medium-sized concert hall
= White Wave Art Hall: Small 193-seat venue
= White Wave Gallery: Space for Various Exhibitions
= Book Publishing White Wave: The Center of Cultural Content Creation
= Bookstore Book and Music: A Place where Books and Music Blend

the best sound facilities
The pride of the White Wave Art Center is excellent sound facilities. Each concert hall is equipped with a specially designed reflector and sound system in consideration of the reverberation and reverberation of sound. Thanks to this, you can enjoy rich sounds anywhere in the grandstand.

a variety of performances and exhibitions
Various genres of performances will be held here, from classical concerts to musicals, plays, book concerts, and fan meetings. In the gallery, you can see various works of art, including paintings, sculptures, installation art, and photography.

Convenient accessibility
Another advantage of the White Wave Art Center is its excellent accessibility. It's a minute's walk from Seocho Station on Subway Line 2, so you can easily visit it by public transportation.

Finish
The White Wave Art Center is a special place where art and everyday life meet beyond just cultural spaces. If you want to take a break in the busy city life and feel the scent of culture, why don't you visit here? Create your own special cultural experience at the White Wave Art Center!

reviews.text:
A little over a month ago, I finally crossed the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) Seoul off my must-visit list. As a venue dedicated to showcasing both established masters and the vibrant contemporary scene, the MMCA is a truly world-class institution.
The most satisfying aspect of the visit was finally standing before works that feel legendary. Nam June Paik's Junk TV (잡동사니 벽) is an anarchic, mesmerizing wall of visual noise that beautifully captures the artist's genius and prescience regarding media overload. It remains a chaotic, vital masterpiece that anchors the modern collection.
Equally compelling, though in a profoundly quieter way, was Do Ho Suh's Floor. The simple act of walking across the glass surface, supported by hundreds of tiny, straining figures, transforms the space into an interactive, existential metaphor. It's a testament to Suh's ability to imbue architectural space with deep, personal meaning.
However, the highlight of the visit, and a thrilling discovery for me, was Jung Yeondoo's Cinemagician. Experiencing this piece for the first time was genuinely captivating. Jung has a powerful way of blending the real and the imagined, and Cinemagician offered a fresh perspective on narrative and memory. It was the perfect example of the MMCA's strength: honoring foundational artists while actively championing the next generation of visionary creators.
The collection is diverse, the curation is thoughtful, and the combination of monumental installations and unexpected delights makes it an absolutely essential stop for anyone interested in contemporary art.

We visited last year and were a bit disappointed in the exhibits. Our friend convinced us to attend this year as Kim Tschang-yeul was showing and we are so glad we did. What an incredible show and artist. Another National Icon and his art is highly sought after, so to be able to see so many of his original pieces in one spot was incredible. You can also see some of his work in the main lobby to the Lotte Hotel Seoul after the show finishes. The Gallery itself is extremely large and they've done a great job renovating the old building and creating a large gallery behind it. There is a large cafe in the lobby with limited food options  and lots of large spaces so it never feels too busy. It's free to walk around the main building but depending on the exhibits you will need to purchase tickets, which can be done easily at the museum in person or at a both. I think you can book online too. The price was really low for an exhibit this size and quality.

I loved this visit and the art work on display this time. The grounds and buildings of the museum are really quite interesting in themselves. Busy coffee shop on site as well as a matcha tea shop.

Beautiful place to walk around and experience traditional Seoul. The hanok houses, narrow alleys, and city views make it feel like stepping back in time, especially early in the morning when it’s quiet.
It can get crowded later in the day, but if you go on a weekday or before noon, it’s very peaceful and great for photos. There are small cafes, galleries, and hidden viewpoints along the way, so it’s fun to explore slowly.
Just remember people actually live here, so be respectful and keep noise down. Overall, a must-visit spot if you want history, culture, and great views all in one walk.

Bukchon Hanok Village is easy to combine with Gyeongbokgung Palace in a day trip. The bus drops you right at Bukchon-ro, where maps help you plan your walk. The village sits on a hillside, so expect some gentle climbs, but the backstreets reveal clusters of traditional hanok homes, rooftop views, and even glimpses of Gyeongbokgung Palace. There are cozy cafes with terraces for a break. Best to allow at least 2 hours to explore and find photo spots. Keep in mind it’s a residential area with access limited to 10 am–5 pm, so be respectful when taking photos. We visited around noon in early January and found it pleasantly uncrowded, though we only managed to see a few hanok houses compared to online photos. Still, it’s worth a visit for the atmosphere and views.

After Korea’s liberation in 1945, this building served as the headquarters for the Ministry of Education and later the Ministry of Culture and Information, becoming the administrative center for national education and cultural policy in the early Republic of Korea.
When those offices moved to Sejong City, the site was reborn in 2012 as the National Museum of Korean Contemporary History.
This makes the museum’s location itself historically meaningful — it’s a place where the modern nation’s governance and cultural identity first took shape.

Inside, the exhibitions are well organized by period, from liberation to the present, making it an excellent introduction to modern Korean history — even for first-time visitors or foreigners.
Its surroundings also add to its significance: right across from Sejong Center and the Government Complex, and just behind it lies Gyeongbokgung Palace and Mt. Bukak. Together they form the symbolic axis of Korea’s politics and history.

One place you absolutely shouldn’t miss is the rooftop observatory on the 8th floor.
From there, you can enjoy a panoramic view of the entire Gyeongbokgung Palace, beautifully framed by the surrounding mountains.
It offers a perfect vantage point to appreciate the geomantic (Pungsu-jiri) harmony of the palace’s location — encircled by mountains that were believed to protect the king and ensure the dynasty’s stability.
It’s not just a museum; it’s a window into Korea’s landscape of power and tradition.

Highly recommended — especially the rooftop view that reveals the deeper meaning of Gyeongbokgung’s setting.

It’s about a 10-minute walk to the main train line, with plenty of coffee shops and convenience stores nearby. There’s also a Olive Young right next to the hotel.

The hotel is generally clean and well-maintained, but our stay was far from pleasant. The biggest issue was the air conditioning—no matter how we adjusted the settings, the room temperature remained at 26°C both day and night. This made it uncomfortably warm for a good night’s sleep. When I asked for assistance, the only suggestion was to turn off the air conditioning entirely. While this did lower the temperature slightly, the lack of airflow made the room feel stuffy and suffocating, eventually causing headaches.

Additionally, the double-bed rooms come with only one blanket, which may not be ideal for some couples. When I requested an extra one, I was informed that hotel policy does not allow for additional blankets. Instead, they provided me with the address of a nearby mall where I could purchase one myself. This was the first time I’ve ever had to buy my own blanket while staying at a three start hotel.

Overall, while the hotel meets basic cleanliness standards, these issues made for a very uncomfortable experience.

Free museum. Several floors, with exhibits on 5th and 3rd. Interactive kids on 4th. Interior room with a view, and on the 8th floor roof outdoor viewing of the palace and Blue House.  couple cafes and areas to sit and rest. The exhibitions were nice, with some English translations.

After Korea’s liberation in 1945, this building served as the headquarters for the Ministry of Education and later the Ministry of Culture and Information, becoming the administrative center for national education and cultural policy in the early Republic of Korea.
When those offices moved to Sejong City, the site was reborn in 2012 as the National Museum of Korean Contemporary History.
This makes the museum’s location itself historically meaningful — it’s a place where the modern nation’s governance and cultural identity first took shape.

Inside, the exhibitions are well organized by period, from liberation to the present, making it an excellent introduction to modern Korean history — even for first-time visitors or foreigners.
Its surroundings also add to its significance: right across from Sejong Center and the Government Complex, and just behind it lies Gyeongbokgung Palace and Mt. Bukak. Together they form the symbolic axis of Korea’s politics and history.

One place you absolutely shouldn’t miss is the rooftop observatory on the 8th floor.
From there, you can enjoy a panoramic view of the entire Gyeongbokgung Palace, beautifully framed by the surrounding mountains.
It offers a perfect vantage point to appreciate the geomantic (Pungsu-jiri) harmony of the palace’s location — encircled by mountains that were believed to protect the king and ensure the dynasty’s stability.
It’s not just a museum; it’s a window into Korea’s landscape of power and tradition.

Highly recommended — especially the rooftop view that reveals the deeper meaning of Gyeongbokgung’s setting.

A well-known luxury department store located in the vibrant Sinchon area of Seoul, South Korea.

It offers a wide variety of high-end fashion, cosmetics, accessories, and household items from both international and Korean brands.

The store is popular for its premium shopping experience, with customer service and product quality being top priorities.

In addition to shopping, Hyundai Department Store Sinchon also has a range of dining options, including cafes and restaurants located within the building, offering both Korean and international cuisine.

There’s also a food court in the basement that provides quick and affordable meals. The store often holds seasonal sales, so checking ahead for any promotions could be beneficial.

The department store is easily accessible by public transportation, with Sinchon Station (Subway Line 2) located nearby. It’s also within walking distance of Ewha Womans University and Yonsei University, making it a popular destination for students and tourists alike.

There’s parking available for those driving, but it can get crowded on weekends and holidays, so public transport is often the better option.

The store’s operating hours usually range from 10:30 AM to around 8:00 PM, but it’s always good to confirm times beforehand.
